These results confirm its robustness and accuracy, offering an effective tool for aquaculture water-quality and risk management.

rows.title: PyFlood: Rapid high-resolution coastal flood mapping with digital elevation model, land cover and water level data
rows.abstract: This study presents a Python-based static flood model (PyFlood) that rapidly generates high resolution coastal flood maps using digital elevation models, land cover, and water level data. PyFlood reduces systematic overestimation in static models through four advances: a hybrid hydro-connectivity algorithm integrating topography and land cover, spatially varying water levels estimated by kriging with external drift using topography and bathymetry, attenuation distance computed from all permanent water bodies, and land-cover-based attenuation calibrated with high water marks using Bayesian optimization. The model was calibrated and validated in the Houston–Galveston region of Texas for Hurricane Ike (2008), and its transferability was evaluated using high water marks from Hurricane Harvey (2017). Results show strong agreement with a physics-based numerical model, substantially lower root mean square error against high water marks than an existing static model (0.507 m versus 3.412 m), and high computational efficiency, supporting emergency forecasting and response during coastal floods.

rows.title: A cloud-based JupyterHub platform for community research with the NextGen water resources modeling framework
rows.abstract: This research integrates existing cyberinfrastructure tools and modeling workflows to support application of the Next Generation Water Resources Modeling Framework (NextGen) for research-scale subdomains across the U.S. We linked the CUAHSI HydroShare data and model repository to the CIROH-2i2c JupyterHub cloud computing platform to establish a flexible, scalable, collaborative environment for research applications of NextGen. This approach allows a user to configure, calibrate, run, and analyze the results from research instances of models formulated for the NextGen framework. Comparison of outputs to retrospective National Water Model (NWM) results and ground-based observations using best-practice community evaluation tools hosted in the cloud software environment serve as a starting point for research to improve NextGen models. The cyberinfrastructure and workflows developed lower barriers for engaging with NextGen models targeting improvement of the NWM.

rows.title: New extensions of Cell2Fire software for fire risk analysis and evaluation in Chilean forests
rows.abstract: Spatial simulation of wildfires is a valuable tool for fire management, supporting both prevention and operational decision-making. However, many existing tools are not publicly available or require restrictive licenses. This paper introduces C2FK, an open-source simulator designed to model fire growth across Chilean landscapes and generate burn probability maps through iterative, spatially explicit simulations. Built on the Cell2Fire engine, C2FK integrates an adaptation of KITRAL, Chile’s national fire behavior system. The implementation includes new equations to estimate rate of spread and length-to-breadth ratio as functions of wind speed, using an elliptical fire growth model. It also incorporates a crown fire behavior module, extending predictive capacity beyond surface fires. We evaluate C2FK by comparing its outputs against synthetic and real wildfire scenarios, demonstrating accuracy and scalability. Cross-platform and parallel-computing enabled, C2FK provides a flexible, high-performance solution to support risk assessment, scenario analysis, and wildfire planning in Chile and other fire-prone environments.

rows.title: On the complementary roles of XVARS and SHAP in explainable AI
rows.abstract: Explainable AI (XAI) is a rapidly expanding field, with methods such as SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP becoming a standard for feature attribution. However, existing approaches face challenges related to limited explanatory power, computational efficiency, scalability, and sensitivity to sampling variability. We have recently developed Explainer VARS (XVARS), a novel XAI framework grounded in global sensitivity analysis, designed to overcome these challenges in a model-agnostic manner. In this paper, we comprehensively compare XVARS with Kernel and Tree SHAPs across multiple machine learning (ML) methods to assess their relative characteristics and performance. Results demonstrate that XVARS requires less than 10% of the computational time needed by SHAP for typical ML problems, consistent with theoretical expectations: XVARS computations are essentially independent of training sample size, whereas both SHAP-based approaches scale linearly with it. We also find that whereas Tree SHAP demonstrates higher efficiency than XVARS for moderate-sized datasets, its performance remains dependent on data volume and different tree model structures and, since the scalability threshold at which its computational cost exceeds that of XVARS is not yet well understood, we leave that as an open question. Meanwhile, XVARS exhibits greater robustness to sampling variability and yields more reliable feature importance estimates, owing to its characterization of the entire input–output space globally rather than focusing only on local neighbourhoods around observed samples, as in SHAPs.

rows.title: Multilayer perceptron model for predicting conservative solute transport in streams and rivers
rows.abstract: Contamination events such as spills and post-fire runoff affect water quality in streams and rivers, and physically based solute transport modeling has been used to predict how such events propagate downstream. However, predicting contaminant transport in these ecosystems remains challenging because model parameters cannot be consistently predicted using readily available site characteristics, such as width, depth, or discharge, through analytical or empirical equations. As a result, standard modeling approaches rely on site- and flow-specific a posteriori calibrations that effectively reproduce past events, but offer limited predictive capabilities. We present a machine learning approach for predicting conservative solute breakthrough curves (BTCs) using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) trained on synthetic and experimental data. To support this effort, we first developed the Tracer Injection Experiments in Rivers and Streams (TIERRAS) database, the largest compilation of conservative solute transport experiments across contrasting hydrogeomorphic characteristics to date. We augmented TIERRAS with synthetic BTCs generated from realistically constrained solutions of the one-dimensional advection-dispersion equation. The MLP model accurately captured solute transport dynamics, requiring ∼1000 synthetic, noise-free BTCs to achieve a cross-correlation score above 0.95 during training. Fine-tuning an MLP pretrained on 3000 synthetic BTCs with 121 experimental BTCs yielded the best generalization, achieving a cross-correlation score of 0.72 for unseen experimental data. These results highlight the potential of deep learning for robust, site-independent, and real-time prediction of solute transport processes, as well as the importance of expanding experimental databases, such as TIERRAS, to support future advances.

rows.title: Editorial Board
Open visual programming extensions in KNIME for reproducible earth observation analytics: Integrating google earth engine with geospatial analytics
rows.abstract: Open Earth observation (EO) archives and cloud processing engines have expanded EO-enabled environmental analytics. However, reproducible and replicable integration between cloud remote-sensing workflows and local geoinformation modelling remains difficult for interdisciplinary users, particularly across multiple tools and scripts. We present KNIME extensions for Google Earth Engine (GEE) and geospatial analytics: open no/low-code visual components that expose core GEE objects as executable nodes and enable interoperability between cloud and local computation. This democratizes end-to-end EO analytics by coupling scalable cloud processing with KNIME's data-science ecosystem for validation and reporting. Three reusable templates demonstrate (1) land-cover mapping, (2) heat-exposure and healthcare-accessibility burden screening, and (3) multimodal GenAI place-type inference from imagery and building data. The software turns script-centric pipelines into transparent, versioned components that support reproducibility and replicability (R&R) and reinforce FAIR, end-to-end environmental workflows.

rows.title: CNN-BiLSTM with attention mechanism and soil-aware dynamic EI-D thresholds for extreme rainfall-induced landslide early warning in subtropical mountains
rows.abstract: Mountainous regions face increasing landslide risks due to climate change-driven extreme rainfall. Existing deep learning methods often fall short in capturing the complex hydro-mechanical processes and soil-specific hydrological responses leading to these failures. To address this, we developed a novel hybrid CNN-BiLSTM model, enhanced with an attention mechanism and a dynamic, soil-aware rainfall intensity-duration (EI-D) threshold. A key innovation is the refined EI-D model, which incorporates soil-specific decay coefficients (λ) to calculate effective cumulative rainfall intensity (Ieff=∑t=116rte−λ(T−t)). This differentiates the influence of antecedent rainfall in clay (λ = 0.15) versus sandy (λ = 0.30) soils, reflecting their differing hydraulic conductivities. The deep learning framework integrates static geospatial data (12 conditioning factors) with dynamic 16-day time-series data (rainfall, soil moisture) to capture both spatial patterns and bidirectional temporal dependencies. The attention mechanism focuses on the most critical time periods. We validated the model using 366 landslides triggered by the extreme rainfall event in Pingjiang County, China, in June 2024. The integrated model achieved strong performance: AUC-ROC of 0.888 ± 0.009, F1-score of 0.822 ± 0.010, precision of 0.837 ± 0.008, recall of 0.807 ± 0.012, and accuracy of 0.862 ± 0.009. This significantly outperformed CNN-only and Random Forest models. The soil-aware EI-D model improved landslide prediction by approximately 30%, capturing 59.1% of landslides compared to 45.4% with a traditional uniform-threshold model. Furthermore, our coupled warning system correctly identified 80% of landslides within the highest-risk zones. This framework offers a promising approach for climate-adaptive landslide early warning.

rows.title: Integrating lumped hydrological modelling with GIS-based flow accumulation for spatiotemporal streamflow estimation
rows.abstract: Estimating water availability in terms of runoff volume over time and space is crucial for identifying suitable locations for micro-scale rainwater harvesting (RWH) structures such as loose stone check dams and gabions, which are constructed along stream networks. Traditional hydrological assessments often rely on empirical methods, such as the Soil Conservation Service - Curve Number (SCS-CN) method, which have limitations in representing spatial variability in streamflow availability along drainage networks across different time scales. While rainfall-runoff models can model streamflow at variable time scales, they provide streamflow values only at the outlet of the catchment. To address these gaps under the conditions of limited gauge availability, this study proposes a lumped–spatial hybrid framework that combines a rainfall–runoff model with a GIS-based flow accumulation scheme to estimate spatiotemporally varying streamflow along the drainage network of small-sized catchments. Two rainfall-runoff models, GR4J and TOPMODEL, were selected for streamflow modeling. The combined approach was applied to an experimental catchment of 1150 km2 in the Ovens River in southeast Australia, covering the period from 1999 to 2020. The streamflow models calibrated for the catchment were integrated with a flow accumulation scheme in GIS to develop a grid-based stream discharge accumulation (GSDA) map at a 10 m resolution. The spatiotemporal GSDA maps were analyzed at annual, monthly, and seasonal timescales. Monthly GSDA maps were validated against upstream gauging station data from Bright, Harrislane, and Harrietville, resulting in NSE values of 0.75, 0.75, and 0.72 for GR4J and 0.62, 0.6, and 0.45 for TOPMODEL, respectively. The annual GSDA highlights wet and dry years, while monthly and seasonal maps capture flow peaks, low-flow periods, and temporal runoff trends across the catchment. Unlike the SCS–CN method, which provides simplified runoff estimates, the GSDA framework offers temporally dynamic and spatially explicit insight into streamflow availability relevant for RWH planning. By estimating available water volumes at candidate stream locations and accounting for temporal variability in harvestable runoff, the proposed approach enhances the reliability of RWH site selection and structure design based on water availability.

rows.title: SARvey - survey with SAR: A new Open-Source InSAR Research Software
rows.abstract: Monitoring surface deformation with Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) time series analysis is essential for various geophysical and engineering applications. We present our new open-source research software SARvey which is tailored, but not limited to engineering applications providing various processing options. It builds upon the packages MintPy and MiaplPy and extends them by full spatial resolution analysis of point and distributed scatterer pixels with spatiotemporal phase unwrapping of sparse point data. We provide case studies with both medium and high spatial resolution imagery, which demonstrates its performance for several case studies including the displacement analysis of landslide, dam, high-rise buildings and airport infrastructure. The results from SARvey agree with previously published results for the same case studies, processed using other well-established open-source and proprietary InSAR time series software. Our new software contributes to research integrity and reproducibility in the field of InSAR time series analysis.

rows.title: Dynamic Adaptive Model Predictive Control for Computationally Efficient Real-Time Flood Management
rows.abstract: Urban flood management requires agile regulation of distributed small-scale storage. This study presents a Dynamic Adaptive Model Predictive Control (DAMPC) framework using an Urban Flood Hazard Weighting Score (UFHWS) module. By reconfiguring multi-objective optimization into state-driven, single-objective Quadratic Programming (QP) tasks, the framework reduces theoretical complexity from O(n3) to O(n). Evaluations across 672 scenarios show an average decision latency of 7.58 s, a 2.9-fold efficiency gain over conventional methods. DAMPC achieved peak flow reductions of 16.26% and 18.72% compared to multi-objective and static benchmarks, respectively. Under ±30% precipitation uncertainty, the system maintains robustness with operational variations within tolerances. By combining computational speed with iterative refinement, DAMPC provides a practical decision-support tool for real-time flood control in complex urban water systems.

rows.title: A novel Weibull-based dynamic model with application to streamflow time series
rows.abstract: Hydrometeorological time series are inherently stochastic and exhibit temporal dependence, commonly modeled using Gaussian autoregressive moving average (ARMA) models. However, the normality assumption is often too restrictive for environmental variables such as streamflow, which are nonnegative and right-skewed. We propose the Wei-ARMA model, a new class of ARMA models based on the Weibull distribution that incorporates ARMA components, external regressors, and a link function. A parametric trend test is also introduced, with parameters estimated via the conditional maximum likelihood method. Monte Carlo simulations assess finite-sample performance. An application to streamflow data from the Vacacaí River, Brazil, shows that the proposed model captures key statistical features, avoids unrealistic negative predictions, and outperforms the Gaussian ARMA. Mean absolute percentage errors in in-sample prediction are reduced by 23%, 34%, and 9% for mean, maximum, and minimum monthly streamflow, respectively, relative to the Gaussian ARMA model. The proposed trend test successfully detects monotonic trends.

rows.title: Improving extreme streamflow prediction by integrating CEEMDAN, autoencoders, and attention-enhanced BiLSTM optimized via GSA-PSO
rows.abstract: This study proposes a novel integrated model, AuGPatt-BiLSTM, to address low accuracy in predicting extreme streamflow. The model integrates Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN) for decomposing series into Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs), autoencoders for denoising, and attention-enhanced Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM) optimized by a hybrid Gravitational Search Algorithm (GSA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Using daily Yellow River flows (1962–2020), CEEMDAN captures nonlinearity and autoencoders preserve high-frequency information. GSA-PSO optimizes BiLSTM hyperparameters to eliminate manual tuning, while attention targets extreme events. Results show the Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE) reached 0.90 and 0.88 at Tongguan and Huaxian stations, respectively. Compared to traditional BiLSTM, the Mean Absolute Relative Error (MARE) for peak flows decreased by 41% and 28%. Furthermore, the model's generalizability was validated using datasets from the United States (Jacob Fork and Animas River), confirming its applicability to varying watershed scales.

rows.title: Hydrological and hydrodynamic decision support tools for assessing nature-based flood solutions: Technical modelling recommendations and challenges
rows.abstract: Nature-based solutions (NbS) are vital for sustainable flood risk management. However, integrating NbS into hydrological and hydrodynamic models is challenged by methodological and computational constraints. This study highlights NbS modelling challenges and offers technical recommendations for improved representation. NbS are categorized into landscape, storage, and diversion types, each requiring different modelling frameworks. Semi-distributed rainfall–runoff models suit preliminary assessments of landscape interventions, while storage and diversion measures demand high-resolution 2D hydrodynamic or Rain-on-Grid models to capture spatial inundation and flow dynamics. 1D hydrodynamic models may have significant limitations to simulate some nature-based solutions. Advancing NbS modelling calls for multi-dimensional, scale-aware frameworks with adaptive parameterization and dynamic mesh refinement to overcome data gaps and computational limits. Physical modelling and field studies remain essential for validating vegetation–hydraulics interactions. This synthesis provides a comprehensive framework and guidance for NbS simulation, highlighting future priorities.

rows.title: SWATtunR: A transparent and reproducible workflow for scripted SWAT+ calibration in R
rows.abstract: This paper introduces SWATtunR, a GitHub-hosted R package for scripted workflows designed to streamline and enhance the calibration and validation process of SWAT + hydrological models. Addressing widespread challenges in model reproducibility, transparency, and user control, SWATtunR integrates both soft and hard calibration workflows within a fully scriptable and procedurally reproducible environment. The tool supports expert-guided and automated workflows, enabling flexible model calibration through parameter sampling, performance evaluation, and advanced visualization. A demonstration using the Little River Experimental Watershed presents its functionality and effectiveness. In this case study, the proposed workflow achieved very good streamflow simulation performance during calibration (NSE >0.65, KGE >0.75, |PBIAS| < 10%) and satisfactory performance during validation, markedly improving upon the uncalibrated model. By promoting transparent and reproducible calibration practices, SWATtunR provides a practical tool for hydrological modelling studies and supports reliable, policy-relevant water resource assessments.

rows.title: Comparative evaluation of DYNA-CLUE and a python-based machine learning framework for long-term land-use and land-cover simulation
rows.abstract: Accurate simulation of land-use and land-cover change (LUCC) is essential for understanding landscape dynamics and supporting environmental decision-making. This study compares DYNA-CLUE with a Python-based LUCC framework (PBLCF) under identical demand, driver, and validation conditions. Unlike regression-based CLUE approaches that derive suitability mainly from a single baseline map, PBLCF learns transition behavior from two temporal land-cover maps using Random Forest and embeds these transition probabilities within a demand-constrained allocation process. This provides a simpler and more flexible hyperparameter structure for controlling transition intensity, scenario-based change, and unrealistic conversions. LUCC Results show that PBLCF achieves higher predictive accuracy (OA = 0.864; Kappa = 0.815) than DYNA-CLUE and improves representation of ecotonal and disturbance-driven classes by capturing non-linear interactions among drivers. In addition, class-specific constraints enhance the persistence of stable land-use types, reducing unrealistic transitions. The framework demonstrates improved long-term stability and provides a flexible, reproducible approach for scenario-based LUCC simulation.

rows.title: Reservoir inflow forecasting using a large language model and time series approach
rows.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer new opportunities, but their application in hydrological modelling remains limited. This study introduces the TIME-LLM framework, using structured prompts to guide an LLM in forecasting daily reservoir inflow. The prompts include task instructions, dataset statistics, and dataset context based on runoff yield and concentration mechanisms that incorporate climatic conditions, underlying surface characteristics, and human activities. Results show that the optimal prompt reduced the model's MAE and RMSE during the calibration period by 17.67% and 16.59%, respectively, while increasing NSE and KGE by 4.18% and 2.69%. During the validation period, MAE and RMSE decreased by 19.88% and 13.83%, respectively, while NSE and KGE improved by 7.29% and 0.34%. TIME-LLM captures temporal patterns in inflow series and recognizes hydrological prompts with reliability. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of applying LLMs to hydrological forecasting and suggest that prompt-based modelling may represent a new paradigm for data-driven environmental modelling.

rows.title: Evaluating rule induction algorithms for scenario discovery
rows.abstract: Scenario discovery translates large simulation ensembles into interpretable input regions linked to policy-relevant outcomes. While previous studies have compared scenario discovery algorithms, they were ad hoc and hard to reproduce. We propose a general workflow to evaluate rule induction methods for scenario discovery. The workflow (i) provides synthetic benchmarks that expose axis and directional misalignment, nonlinearity, boundary fuzziness, and dimensional noise; (ii) unifies metrics and diagnostics around coverage–density trade-offs, interpretability, runtime, and scaling; and (iii) prescribes a staged experiment design from low-dimensional screening to stress testing. We illustrate the approach by comparing established algorithms PRIM and CART with an oblique decision tree variant called HHCART(D), finding that the latter does not outperform the former. Our workflow surfaces method-specific trade-offs and supports principled, reproducible algorithm selection for scenario discovery.

rows.title: Sensitivity and uncertainty in habitat suitability modeling: guidance and pitfalls for ecological applications
rows.abstract: Habitat suitability index (HSI) models are common tools for predicting species’ habitat requirements and informing management actions. Application of HSI models is widespread in ecological research and ecosystem restoration, but many HSI models were developed prior to the establishment and use of modern model evaluation methods, and few have been evaluated for uncertainty or sensitivity. We performed global sensitivity and uncertainty analyses on 349 blue book HSI models available in the ecorest R-package. Our results suggest that many HSI models in ecorest are not sensitive to all model inputs. Further, the complexity and structure of HSI models and their parameters influenced both model sensitivity and uncertainty. Our results emphasize the importance of rigorously testing HSI models to ensure that model structure facilitates rather than hinders model performance. Thorough evaluation of uncertainty and sensitivity can help ensure that models produce reliable and informative results to guide conservation and management decisions.

rows.title: Scaling open-weight large language models for hydropower regulatory information extraction: A systematic analysis
rows.abstract: Information extraction from regulatory and technical documents using large language models (LLMs) involves practical trade-offs between extraction quality and computational cost. We evaluate eight open-weight LLMs spanning 0.6B–70B parameters on hydropower licensing documents and report deployment-oriented evidence under a unified extraction schema and evaluation protocol. Across the model set, we observe clear scale-dependent trends in both baseline extraction quality and the effectiveness of reflective reasoning (self-checking) under our fixed-prompt, no-augmentation setting. Mid-scale models often provide a favorable balance of accuracy and efficiency, whereas the smallest models show limited or inconsistent gains from the reasoning variants tested. Larger models achieve the highest overall F1 scores but incur substantially greater compute and infrastructure requirements. We further find that reliability failure modes can distort conventional metrics in this domain: in particular, high recall can coincide with systematic extraction errors when models fabricate values for fields that are absent from the source text, underscoring the importance of conservative null handling and evidence-grounded evaluation. Overall, our study provides a reproducible resource–performance comparison for open-weight LLM-based extraction in hydropower regulatory documentation and offers practical guidance for model selection under different deployment constraints.

rows.title: Community-oriented data integration and communication framework for streamflow forecast models and flood inundation map products
rows.abstract: Access to critical flood risk information is often constrained by expert-driven workflows that require specialized software, creating barriers to stakeholder engagement and effective science communication. This study presents a generalized web-based framework that integrates federal datasets to support real-time and scenario-based flood forecasting and mapping across the continental United States. Using client-side technologies including WebAssembly, Web Workers, and IndexedDB, we developed an on-demand geoprocessing framework that generates flood inundation maps directly in the browser. Flood maps can be generated from National Water Model forecast outputs and Office of Water Prediction Flood Inundation Mapping products. The framework also applies FEMA Hazus damage assessment methods to property data from the National Structure Inventory. A case study of the 2019 Midwestern floods shows the platform's practical value for emergency managers, planners, and communities conducting flood risk assessments.

rows.title: Semi-implicit time integration of the Exner equation for bedload transport over a non-erodible layer: Application to a tidal sandbank model
rows.abstract: Existing morphodynamic models that consider bedload sediment transport over non-erodible layers often rely on small morphological time steps or numerical filtering techniques for stability. A time-integration method of the Exner equation that can simulate bedform evolution over large timescales without relying on numerical fixes appears to be lacking. In this research, we provide two semi-implicit time-integration methods and propose a method to incorporate the non-erodible layer without numerical fixes, applied to a tidal sandbank model. As shown by our results, both methods work well, and are computationally fast. The newly developed model is compared against a conventional approach, which violates the non-erodibility condition, is computationally less efficient due to the need for small time steps, and introduces new uncertainty by adding more parameters. Our new method to deal with the non-erodibility allows for large morphological time steps and is a suitable method to study tidal sandbank dynamics in sediment-scarce environments.

rows.title: Pyenspp: A Python package for ensemble precipitation forecast post-processing using a hybrid KAN–CSGD model
rows.abstract: Reliable and accurate prediction of precipitation is of great practical value. Focusing on the post-processing of ensemble precipitation forecasts from numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, this paper introduces Pyenspp—a Python package that integrates preprocessing, calibration, dependence reconstruction, and verification into a unified workflow. Specifically, the package enables extraction of area-weighted precipitation forecasts, supports three transformation methods to mitigate precipitation skewness, and implements ensemble calibration using both quantile mapping (QM) and the proposed Kolmogorov–Arnold Network–Censored Shifted Gamma Distribution (KAN–CSGD) model. The Schaake Shuffle (SS) is incorporated to restore temporal coherence across lead times, and comprehensive verification metrics are provided. Case study results demonstrate that KAN–CSGD effectively reduces bias and improves forecast reliability compared to raw forecasts, outperforming QM. The SS further enhances forecast skill for accumulated precipitation across lead times. Pyenspp offers a practical, extensible tool for environmental prediction and management.

rows.title: Modeling the impact of natural obstructions and bed topography on hydraulic efficiency in free water surface wetlands
rows.abstract: Hydraulic efficiency in free water surface (FWS) constructed wetlands can be reduced by obstructions, sedimentation, and microtopographic variability, which disrupt flow paths and create dead zones. This study extends a standard 2D depth-averaged hydraulic model with slope-sensitive roughness. The formulation enables spatially explicit simulation of terrain-driven resistance. The framework is computationally efficient, modular, and reproducible. It enables rapid testing of alternative configurations under diverse boundary conditions. We simulated synthetic scenarios with varied obstructions (sediment, vegetation) and bed topographies. This evaluated their impact on flow distribution, residence time, and efficiency. Inlet obstructions and clustered vegetation reduced retention. Lateral vegetation preserved flow corridors. Transverse topography enhanced mixing. Staged gradients improved retention. Excessive or chaotic roughness fragmented circulation and promoted early breakthrough. This modeling approach is transferable. It evaluates wetland hydraulic function and supports design optimization.

rows.title: A hierarchical decision framework for low-cost sensor deployment in lake monitoring under uncertainty
rows.abstract: Low-cost sensors (LCS), such as compact electrochemical and optical probes for monitoring water-quality indicators, enable rapid water-quality data collection but face deployment challenges due to high uncertainty. This study proposes a hierarchical framework integrating quality–quantity analysis, Value of Information (VOI), and complex network refinement. In Stage I, an optimal sampling density grade (hereafter referred to as grade, a classified discrete grade characterizing sampling intensity, unitless) is selected via mutual information-confidence interval (MI–CI) analysis. A subsequent Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA)-based adjustment refines the spatial distribution of candidate sites, yielding the final deployment scale N∗. In Stage II, candidate sites are prioritized using VOI, with coverage and structural gains as modifiers. Validated on Lake Taihu, China, across multiple periods and uncertainty scenarios, the framework improves hotspot identification compared to expert-based methods. By decoupling grade selection from spatial prioritization, it provides a transparent approach for robust LCS deployment under uncertainty.

rows.title: RiverFlood-1D v 1.0: coupling parabolic and backwater (PAB) scheme and Muskingum-Cunge model for river flood routing, with application to the Po River (Italy)
rows.abstract: RiverFlood-1D is a discharge routing model for simulating flood wave propagation in rivers with arbitrary cross-section geometries. It couples the parabolic-backwater (PAB) scheme with the Muskingum-Cunge (MC) approach, dynamically updating routing parameters at each computational step based on steady water surface profiles that account for downstream conditions. The model was verified against four test cases, including compound channels, mixed flow regimes, and a dam-break experiment with highly irregular cross sections. It was then applied to a real flood event along a 60 km reach of the Po river (Italy, April 2009), achieving mean absolute percentage errors of 0.230 and 0.119 for discharge and water depth, respectively, comparable to HEC-RAS (0.210 and 0.080). RiverFlood-1D remained stable in the dam-break test where HEC-RAS's unsteady solver failed to converge. The model combines accuracy similar to full dynamic-wave solvers with greater numerical robustness, making it well suited for operational, real-time flood-forecasting applications.

rows.title: Quadratic decomposition and WOA-optimized CNN-ResNet-BiGRU-Attention: A novel hybrid framework for hydrological runoff forecasting
rows.abstract: Accurate and reliable monthly runoff prediction is a crucial component of scientific water resources management. Due to the impacts of human activities and climate change, runoff series exhibit non-stationarity, which typically deteriorates the performance of most existing runoff prediction models. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel hydrological runoff forecasting model based on double decomposition and deep learning. The model first decomposes the runoff series using Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN). Then, the K-Means algorithm classifies the subsequences according to the sample entropy criterion and frequency characteristics. The Singular Spectrum Analysis-Variational Mode Decomposition (SSA-VMD) model is introduced to conduct a secondary decomposition of the high-frequency components. Subsequently, a CNN-ResNet-BiGRU model integrated with the Attention mechanism is optimized by the Whale Optimization Algorithm (WOA) to simulate and predict the runoff series. The results of the monthly runoff series at the Longmen Hydrological Station in the Yellow River Basin demonstrate that the Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency (NSE) coefficient of the proposed model reaches 0.9743. Compared with the single VMD decomposition model, the Mean Squared Error (MSE) of the double decomposition model is reduced by 80.86%, and the NSE is increased by 18.27%. Moreover, simulation predictions at three hydrological stations in different regions of the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River Basin further verify the model's potential applicability, with all NSE values exceeding 0.95. This study provides an effective approach for monthly runoff prediction in non-stationary environments, which is of great significance for flood control and scientific water resources management.

rows.title: A simulated annealing optimization framework to reduce positional uncertainty and improve performance of species distribution models
rows.abstract: Positional uncertainty in species occurrence records refers to the deviation of geographic coordinates from their true locations. Such uncertainty can reduce both the predictive accuracy and ecological interpretability of species distribution models. We proposed a simulated annealing optimization framework that iteratively adjusts geographic coordinates to maximize model performance and the ecological plausibility of response curves, which can be flexibly embedded into different species distribution models. Using MaxEnt (Maximum entropy model) as a case study, we validated the framework on Ailuropoda melanoleuca (A. melanoleuca) and virtual species datasets. The results demonstrate that coordinates optimization significantly enhances the discriminative capacity of multiple species distribution models. Additionally, the characteristics of the morphology of the primary response curves are enhanced. Predictions from optimized lower-precision data show minimal differences compared with predictions based on high-precision data. This approach provides a feasible solution to reduce positional uncertainty in species distribution modeling.

rows.title: Hybrid geometry-aware PSO–ODT for terrain meshing in complex terrain
rows.abstract: Wind-field simulation over complex terrain requires terrain meshes that capture local topographical variations while remaining suitable for numerical preprocessing. This study proposes a geometry-aware terrain mesh optimization framework coupling Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) with Optimal Delaunay Triangulation (ODT). To improve search efficiency, the three-dimensional terrain optimization problem is reduced to a two-dimensional one: terrain points are projected onto a plane, optimized in the projected space, and reconstructed in three-dimensional space using Kriging interpolation. A terrain-density weight is embedded into the two-dimensional ODT energy to introduce salient three-dimensional terrain information and guide local mesh redistribution. The method was evaluated using aspect ratio, radius ratio, minimum angle, and a comparative downstream CFD case. The results showed improved mesh regularity and locally refined terrain representation while maintaining generally consistent main flow-field patterns, indicating its potential as a reproducible preprocessing strategy for complex-terrain wind-field simulations.

rows.title: UQEF-Dynamic: A scalable open-source tool for forward uncertainty quantification and global sensitivity analysis of time-varying model outputs
rows.abstract: This work presents UQEF-Dynamic, an open-source Python tool for forward uncertainty quantification and sensitivity analysis of models with time-varying outputs, such as hydrological and environmental systems. Existing tools rarely handle high-dimensional, computationally expensive models with vectorial or functional outputs, nor do they fully exploit modern high-performance computing. UQEF-Dynamic addresses these gaps with a scalable, portable framework supporting sampling-based methods and non-intrusive Polynomial Chaos Expansion (PCE), extended with Karhunen–Loève (KL) surrogates to reduce output dimensionality, and enabling time-varying and generalized Sobol’ sensitivity indices. Alongside the software, this work provides a unified treatment of the underlying mathematical methods. We demonstrate the framework through two case studies: an analysis of the HBV-SASK hydrological model, to our knowledge the most comprehensive analysis of this model, and the construction of a KL–PCE surrogate for a 24-dimensional electrochemical battery model. Results show that UQEF-Dynamic delivers efficient analysis and deeper insight into model behavior under varying conditions.

rows.title: A review of optimization systems and methods for wastewater treatment plants operation
rows.abstract: Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) play a critical role in managing sewage before it is released into the environment. As regulations become more stringent, plants must adapt to these changes, making the development of innovative methodologies for optimizing WWTPs essential. This work provides an overview of how WWTP operation optimization can be conducted. First, the fundamental aspects of WWTP processes, modeling, and operation are presented, along with the basics of optimization problems. This article then explores the application of WWTP operation optimization within the literature, starting with the formulation of the problem, followed by the methods used for optimization. The interaction between optimization systems and the plant, as well as their degree of implementation, is examined. Finally, the current developments and the existing gaps to obtain more complete and applicable optimization systems are discussed.

rows.title: A bi-level hybrid MOEA-ε-MP framework for large-scale multi-objective water network scheduling and allocation
rows.abstract: Water networks connect rivers, lakes, diversion projects, and storage works, and their scheduling-allocation must address structural and functional complexity. This study develops a water-society-ecology synergy-based integrated water-network scheduling-allocation (WSE-IWNSA) model and proposes a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm-ε-constraint-mathematical programming solver framework (MOEA-ε-MP) for large-scale multi-objective problems. Algorithmic performance of the framework is evaluated on two test problems by comparing two hybrid variants, H-Gurobi and H-COPT, with two standalone MOEAs. Practical applicability is further examined in the Shaanxi case using H-Gurobi. In the test problems, MOEA-ε-MP shows faster observed convergence than standalone MOEAs; more objectives tend to slow convergence and increase fluctuations; and H-Gurobi/H-COPT generally achieve better observed hypervolume, inverted generational distance, and inverted generational distance plus. In the case study, the WSE-IWNSA model delivers simultaneous improvements in water supply and ecological satisfaction. Overall, the proposed WSE-IWNSA model and MOEA-ε-MP framework provide an effective approach for large-scale multi-objective optimization of complex water networks.

rows.title: GIFIS: A generalized immersive flood information system specification
rows.abstract: This study introduces Generalized Immersive Flood Information Specification (GIFIS), a vendor-agnostic, JSON Schema–based framework for encoding, validating, and exchanging hydrologic and environmental data for reproducible and interoperable virtual and augmented reality applications. By defining standardized semantics for entities such as sensor datasets, hydrological model outputs, warnings and alerts, and infrastructure assets, along with portable document types for spatial anchoring, scene composition, and evidence packaging, GIFIS transforms interoperability into a verifiable property of the data itself. A built-in validator enforces conformance through rule codes and machine-readable diagnostics, ensuring that information published once can be deterministically interpreted across analytical, operational, and immersive environments. Through its schema-centric and engine-neutral design, GIFIS enables any client to load and interpret hydrologic information without reliance on proprietary rendering pipelines or manual data harmonization for immersive platforms and applications. By coupling semantic rigor with open governance and extensibility, GIFIS establishes a sustainable foundation for transparent, FAIR-compliant flood information systems that bridge scientific research, operational decision support, and public communication.

rows.title: Generative diffusion model for environmental diffusion problems
rows.abstract: Modeling pollutant diffusion remains a central challenge in environmental science due to multi-scale processes, incomplete observations and uncertain boundary or initial conditions. We observe close conceptual parallels between generative diffusion models and physical diffusion processes, motivating the adaptation of generative diffusion methods for environmental modeling. We target four canonical tasks: spatiotemporal forecasting, spatial downscaling, data assimilation, and emission/parameter inversion. We provide a systematic mapping between pollutant transport physics and generative diffusion principles, and survey recent applications of diffusion models in environmental contexts. Based on this analysis, we propose four task-specific frameworks—Time-aligned, Corrective, Autoregressive and Deterministic Diffusion—that integrate physical constraints and uncertainty quantification into generative models. We provide conceptual framework prototypes that illustrate how generative diffusion models can achieve physically consistent probabilistic forecasting, bias-corrected downscaling, stable data assimilation, and robust inversion. This work establishes a principled pathway to couple generative diffusion with environmental physics for future empirical and operational studies.

rows.title: PyGREET: A modular Python platform of the GREET life cycle analysis model for technology assessment
rows.abstract: The research and development version of the Greenhouse gases, Regulated Emissions, and Energy use in Technologies (R&D GREET®) model is publicly available and widely used for life cycle analysis (LCA) of energy systems and emerging technologies. However, its current Excel and .NET platforms face scaling and maintenance challenges. This paper introduces PyGREET, a modular Python-based platform designed for scalability and interoperability with other LCA tools. PyGREET's architecture separates domain modeling from numerical solvers, facilitating its maintenance and reusability for web-hosted and standalone derivative applications. Extensive validation across 2,119 technology pathways confirms computational equivalence with current platforms, yielding a negligible mean relative difference of 3.24 × 10−8%. By establishing a robust, modular framework, PyGREET enhances transparency, user experience, and interoperability. This platform provides the foundation for reliable LCA modeling, and the continued expansion of R&D GREET at Argonne with advanced features for technology assessment and informed decision-making.

rows.title: Modelling the human impact on hydrological cycle: The MISDc v3.1 model
rows.abstract: This study presents MISDc v3.1, a process-based, flexible and open-source hydrological model developed to simulate complex water dynamics in large and human-impacted river systems. The model is applied to the Po River basin, Italy, subjected to strong anthropogenic impact. Calibration uses hydrometeorological data from 2000 to 2023, while validation is performed through multi-variable comparison against observed river discharge and satellite-based measurements of soil moisture, evaporation, snow water equivalent, and irrigation volumes. Quantitative performance assessment indicates strong simulation accuracy across multiple gauge stations (modified Kling–Gupta Efficiency = 0.88–0.93). The inclusion of irrigation and reservoir operation modules markedly enhances river discharge simulations, particularly during low-flow conditions and the 2022–2023 extreme drought. Uncertainty, assessed through the BLUECAT method, fosters a better understanding of model reliability across flow regimes. Owing to its Python-based and open-access architecture, MISDc v3.1 is easily transferable to other basins, offering a robust and flexible tool for integrated water resources management.

rows.title: A framework for reflecting on decisions in the modelling cycle incorporating a fitness-for-purpose and pathway perspective
rows.abstract: Environmental modelling involves many decisions, ranging from choices about scope and boundaries, and which system components to represent, to determining how model results are communicated. However, many of these decisions are not systematically considered, which can undermine the credibility and effectiveness of models. This study introduces a structured framework that considers choices at decision forks in the modelling cycle. We suggest using the concept of fitness-for-purpose and a pathway perspective to reflect on modelling decisions through four steps: a) identification of decision boundaries; b) modelling pathway and reasoning; c) evaluation of modelling decisions; and d) iterative refinement. This approach aims to enhance transparency and effectiveness, going beyond documentation of model design and testing by explicitly documenting the rationale and reasons for each modelling decision. We demonstrate the use of this framework for the case of an eco-hydrological model that simulates vegetation condition to support environmental flow management in the Narran Lakes, Australia.

rows.title: Enhancing high-flow estimation in rainfall-runoff models using resampling techniques: applications to GR4J and Sacramento models
rows.abstract: Floods cause significant damage globally, making accurate flood magnitude estimation crucial. However, limited high-flow observations can affect the skill of conceptual rainfall-runoff models for flood simulations. Data resampling techniques have shown improved model calibration for imbalanced datasets, but do not preserve the temporal structure of time series data needed to correctly represent flood behaviour in conceptual models. Here this issue is addressed by developing a modified Kling-Gupta efficiency (KGE) objective function incorporating resampling methods, specifically over-sampling (OS) and hybrid-sampling (HS). We calibrated the Genie Rural a 4 Parameters Journalier (GR4J) model and the Sacramento Soil Moisture Accounting Model (SAC) across 168 Australian catchments, focusing on flows exceeding the 99.8th percentile. Compared to standard KGE and two high-flow objective functions (i.e., Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency with a penalty term and Annual Peak Flow Bias) our resampling-modified KGE improved high-flow estimation in most catchments, particularly those with lower baseflow indices and higher runoff skewness.

rows.title: Complexity vs. efficiency: Are full-structure Copula models worth the cost in multivariate hydrological simulation?
rows.abstract: Accurate representation of multivariate dependence is essential in environmental stochastic simulation, yet increasing model flexibility often entails substantial computational cost and structural uncertainty. This study evaluates three Copula-based frameworks of increasing complexity: Gaussian/t Copulas (GtC), Dependence Tree Copulas (DTC), and Bayesian model averaging with vine Copulas (BMA-Vine). Using synthetic datasets and hydrological observations, model performance is assessed through correlation reconstruction and multivariate goodness-of-fit (GoF), including the Cramér–von Mises (CvM) statistic and energy distance (ED2). Results show that increased complexity does not consistently ensure superior performance across all data conditions. GtC remains stable for near-elliptical dependence, while DTC offers efficient sparse approximations but may underestimate indirect dependencies. BMA-Vine provides the most robust results, particularly for heterogeneous or tail-dependent structures. Findings suggest model selection should balance flexibility, data characteristics, and computational constraints rather than defaulting to complex vine constructions.

rows.title: Flash flood visual simulation as an online chained service: a data-model-knowledge integrated framework
rows.abstract: Dynamically presenting the progression of flash floods within virtual geographical scenes enhances users' visual perception of flash flood hazards and decision-making efficacy. Existing flash flood simulation methods suffer from slow visual response and difficulties in online service delivery. We propose an online chained service framework for flash flood visual simulation, which integrates data-model-knowledge. First, we build a large language model (LLM)-driven integrated data-model-knowledge correlation framework. Second, we construct knowledge graph-guided construction of online service chain for flash floods simulation. Finally, we developed a B/S-based prototype system and validated it through case studies. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework effectively facilitates online simulation and dynamic rendering of flood evolution. Compared with conventional methods, the average service construction efficiency is improved by 54%. The scene rendering frame rate remains stable above 85 FPS, supporting dynamic queries for critical hydrological information. This method establishes a new paradigm for disaster virtual geographic scene services.

rows.title: A novel series-parallel hybrid method employing fusion of deep features for air quality index forecasting
rows.abstract: This research introduces a novel series-parallel hybrid technique for air quality index (AQI) forecasting by combining an ARFIMA model with a parallel ensemble of LSTM, ConvLSTM, BiLSTM, and CNN architectures. A novel feature fusion method is suggested to improve time series forecasting. The hybrid model can capture linear and nonlinear patterns with statistical modeling and deep feature transformation, employing dimensionality reduction and additive/multiplicative hybrid strategies. The model generates both point and interval forecasts, with forecast error distributions modeled using t location scale and gaussian distributions to construct the prediction intervals. The method is assessed using four-point and four-interval accuracy measures against three hybrid baselines, five deep learning (DL) models, and thirteen machine learning (ML) models. Tests conducted using Delhi AQI data using different train-validation-test splits show that the suggested model performs noticeably better than other ML models at multiple significance levels, exhibiting greater prediction accuracy and resilience.

rows.title: An integrated modeling platform for land-coast-ocean continuum: The Gulf of America coastal hazards forecast system (GAm-CHFS)
rows.abstract: The Mississippi River–Gulf of America continuum supports vital coastal communities and infrastructure but faces increasing exposure to compound coastal hazards. Forecasting across this land–coast–ocean system remains challenging due to complex interactions among hydrological, oceanic, and atmospheric processes. We present the Gulf of America Coastal Hazards Forecast System (GAm-CHFS), an operational modeling framework that integrates land, river, and ocean dynamics through both one-way and dynamically two-way coupling within the COAWST system. This framework enables seamless simulation of watershed–coastal interactions and resolves multiscale processes governing compound flooding, water quality, and biogeochemical dynamics. GAm-CHFS delivers 72-h forecasts of river discharge, coastal water levels, ocean circulation, hypoxia, and carbon fluxes across the Mississippi River Basin and adjacent coastal ocean. Case studies show improved prediction of nonlinear interactions among storm surge, rainfall, and river discharge. This system provides a foundation for AI-enabled, scalable, and uncertainty-aware coastal hazard forecasting.

rows.title: Deep learning meets GPR: Exploring transformer models for precision soil depth prediction
rows.abstract: Accurate soil depth mapping is vital for hydrological and ecological insights, yet traditional methods remain laborious. We integrated ground-penetrating radar (GPR) with a Transformer-based deep learning model to enhance predictions in a steep forested catchment. Using datasets comprising point-scale soil measurements and GPR transects (128 auger, 550 GPR, 678 combined points), we benchmarked the Transformer against neural networks (ANN, DNN) and machine learning models (random forest, support vector machine) under two variable strategies: all variables and Boruta-based selection. The Transformer outperformed all models across datasets and strategies, even with limited auger data. GPR data combined with all variables yielded superior predictions over Boruta-selected variables, indicating features deemed less critical in traditional models retain predictive value in Transformers. Notably, GPR integration revealed significant soil depth reductions at footslopes—undetectable with auger data alone. These findings demonstrate the enhanced accuracy of coupling GPR with Transformer models for soil depth mapping in complex terrains.

rows.title: A novel coupled BN-PLUS-IC model for simulating land use change and carbon emissions under SSP-RCP scenarios: A case study of the Fujian Province, China
rows.abstract: Land use changes shape terrestrial carbon budget, and accurate predictions of land use and associated carbon dynamics are essential for achieving carbon neutrality. This study develops a BN-PLUS-IC model that integrates a Bayesian network (BN) for probabilistic land use demand prediction, the Patch-Generating Land Use Simulation (PLUS) model for gridded patch level spatial allocation, and the IPCC carbon emission coefficient (IC) method for spatially explicit territorial carbon accounting. Applied to Fujian Province, China, under three SSPs (SSP119, SSP245, SSP585) and three GCMs (EC-Earth3-China, GFDL-ESM4-China, MRI-ESM2-China), BN-PLUS-IC yields a FOM of 0.19, PA of 0.36, and UA of 0.22 for BN, and a Kappa coefficient of 0.84 and OA of 0.89 for PLUS on the 2020 reference data. Across the scenario ensemble, construction land, water area, grassland, and bare land generally increase, while forest and cultivated land decline, with urbanization pressure propagating from coastal to inland regions. Net carbon emissions rise from [24.92, 25.79] × 106 t in 2030 to [25.61, 28.50] × 106 t in 2060, with variance decomposition revealing that SSPs dominate long term emissions (84.3-96.5%) while interaction between GCM and SSP dominates in 2030 (62.7%). Sensitivity analysis further identifies the construction land carbon emission coefficient as the single most influential IC parameter. These findings suggest that realizing Fujian's dual carbon goals requires reining in coastal construction land expansion, scaling up blue carbon and forest sink protection inland, and cross-departmental coordination among natural resources, ecology, and forestry agencies.

rows.title: ISEHSD: a feedback-based, integrated social-ecohydrological system dynamic model for studying river basin-level transformation
rows.abstract: Models are essential for representing intertwined socio-ecohydrological interactions that shape human-water systems. River basin is the fundamental unit that links human and nature, yet existing models often struggle to capture basin-specific feedback and support sustainability assessments. We develop the Integrated Social-Ecohydrological System Dynamics (ISEHSD) model, a transferable and extensible framework specially designed for river basin-level analysis. ISEHSD enables sustainability assessment within the basin's biophysical boundaries by explicitly coupling climate dynamics and human interventions across 11 components within a unified feedback structure. We demonstrate a use-case implementation in the Yellow River Basin, a river basin with intensive anthropogenic interference. Simulation results underscore the efficacy of ISEHSD in capturing complex interactions within river basins. Global sensitivity analysis and uncertainty quantification are employed to identify key policy levers and assess trade-offs among alternative policies. ISEHSD provides a scalable and interpretable tool for stakeholder dialogue and sustainable management for global river basins.

rows.title: Short-term forecasting of daily dissolved oxygen in streams using SWAT, remote sensing and explainable machine learning
rows.abstract: Dissolved oxygen (DO) concentration is a key indicator of aquatic ecosystem health yet modelling and forecasting it accurately at daily resolution remains challenging due to the complex interplay of influencing factors. In this study, we explore the potential of combining diverse data sources, including in-situ observations, satellite-derived time series, and modelled catchment flow and nutrient loads from SWAT models, to forecast daily DO concentrations in streams. This is the first study that integrates SWAT-simulated hydrological and nutrient outputs with remote sensing data and machine learning to forecast daily DO in streams, advancing beyond previous models that rely solely on observations or use models only for DO simulation. We evaluated the performance of three widely used machine learning and deep learning models (Random Forest, LSTM, and Transformer) at three stream sites in the Upper Piako catchment in New Zealand. The results showed that model performance varied by site, emphasizing the importance of input variables tailored to local conditions. While water temperature consistently emerged as a dominant predictor, other variables such as baseflow and vegetation indices also were found to be important predictors. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating domain knowledge to guide feature selection, particularly when combining observational, remote sensing, and modelled data, to improve DO forecasting accuracy.

rows.title: Enhancing SWAT-based ecosystem modeling through satellite data and hybrid AI under climate change
rows.abstract: As climate change intensifies, reliable ecosystem models are becoming important for sustainable water management. This study aims to improve SWAT-based ecosystem modeling by minimizing predictive uncertainties in SWAT simulations and providing more reliable streamflow predictions. To assess data source effects, the SWAT model was driven by observational and satellite-based meteorological data, demonstrating the effectiveness of satellite inputs in data-scarce regions. To reduce discrepancies between simulated and observed flows, SWAT-TCN and SWAT-CatBoost models were integrated into a Regime-Adaptive Ensemble (RAE)-based SWAT + TCN–CatBoost framework. Model performance was evaluated using statistical metrics and TOPSIS and VIKOR, while SHAP was used for interpretation. The results indicate that regime-adaptive hybrid approach improved SWAT performance, with RAE Hybrid Model giving the best validation results (NSE = 0.90, KGE = 0.87). Subsequently, the framework was applied to future projections using three GCMs and two SSP scenarios, demonstrating more reliable results under climate change.

rows.title: Coupling agent-based and InVEST® models for spatio-temporal simulation of land-use change effects on ecosystem services
rows.abstract: Understanding socio-ecological systems requires methods that capture spatial and temporal dynamics. Yet, environmental modelling approaches rarely represent both space and time. We developed a coupling framework that conceptualizes how to link dynamic simulation models with static models by letting the dynamic model control the static one. Building on this framework, we created NetVest, a tool that connects NetLogo-based agent-based models with static Python-based InVEST® models. We tested NetVest in a case study on smallholder-driven land-use change and its effects on economic functions and biodiversity. The case study illustrated how examining patterns at multiple time points reveals underlying mechanisms. In conclusion, NetVest enables more realistic modelling of socio-ecological systems by integrating spatial and temporal processes. This supports the design of land-use strategies that balance biodiversity conservation with land-use change.

rows.title: The efficient estimation of Sobol' indices and Shapley effects using random sampling high dimensional model representations and relevance vector machine regression
rows.abstract: Global Sensitivity Analysis (GSA) is a powerful tool for understanding the influence of input variables on model outputs, particularly in complex systems. This paper presents a practical approach for estimating Sobol’ indices and Shapley effects using random sampling high dimensional model representations (RS-HDMR) and relevance vector machine (RVM) regression. The proposed method leverages the properties of RS-HDMR to construct high-fidelity surrogate models that enable algebraic computation of Sobol’ indices and Shapley effects, complementing direct estimation approaches by providing a reusable approximation with interpretable component function decomposition. By mapping RS-HDMR expansion coefficients to Sobol’ indices and Shapley effects, the methodology provides a comprehensive framework for variance based GSA in complex systems. The integration of RVM regression enhances the accuracy and efficiency of estimating RS-HDMR expansion coefficients, making the approach suitable for high-dimensional data. The efficacy of the proposed method is demonstrated through a series of case studies, including the decomposition of benchmark analytic functions and the parameter sensitivity analysis of water quality models. The results indicate that while Sobol’ indices are robust for independent inputs, Shapley effects offer a more nuanced understanding in scenarios with interdependent variables. This dual approach provides a useful utility for practitioners, enabling informed decision-making under uncertainty.

rows.title: River Integrated Observations for Fire-Impacted Network Discovery and Evaluation in R (RIO-FINDER)
rows.abstract: Wildfires increasingly disrupt hydrologic and biogeochemical processes in and across river networks. Logistical and financial constraints continue to limit the duration and spatial extent of studies of fire-impacted river networks, and therefore the identification of broader patterns of hydrologic and water-quality responses post-fire. To address this gap, we developed the River Integrated Observations for Fire-Impacted Network Discovery and Evaluation in R (RIO-FINDER), an open-source framework and application that links four decades of wildfire data with high-resolution hydrologic observations across the coterminous United States. We integrate fire data from the Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS) and high-resolution hydrology observations from the US Geological Survey's National Water Information System (NWIS) through the National Hydrography Dataset Plus (NHDPlus) stream network. This enables users to identify monitoring sites embedded within fire-affected watersheds systematically. RIO-FINDER utilizes the Shiny R package to create an interactive application for visualizing, querying, and exporting custom subsets of the larger dataset. It also features a standalone tool for on-demand assessments of newly burned watersheds that requires only a user-supplied fire perimeter shapefile. By design, RIO-FINDER lowers the barrier to discovering existing water quantity and quality datasets of fire-impacted rivers in the conterminous US, supporting the design of targeted pre- and post-fire monitoring campaigns and a timely understanding of fire impacts on fluvial networks at large spatiotemporal scales.

rows.title: Composite2Change (C2C) on Google Earth Engine: Time-series change detection and metrics characterizing disturbance and recovery
rows.abstract: Satellite time series enable the consistent and scalable characterization of land cover changes and vegetation dynamics across extensive areas. The Composite2Change (C2C) protocol applies temporal spectral trend analysis to identify land change events, producing metrics that describe the timing, magnitude, duration, rate, direction, and recovery dynamics of disturbances. These metrics summarize spectral trajectories and support mapping and modelling applications. While the methods have been published and their value demonstrated, their replication across regions and sensors has been limited due to high storage and computational demands, coupled with the lack of available implementation. To address these barriers, we implemented C2C as a reproducible cloud-native framework within Google Earth Engine (C2C-GEE). C2C-GEE enables users to generate change products and metrics that describe the spectral and temporal signatures of land cover change and recovery. The framework supports the transparent and systematic generation of standardized change metrics for large-area mapping and modelling applications worldwide.

rows.title: OpenEOcraft: A generic R-based framework for earth observation data cubes analysis
rows.abstract: The openEO initiative provides a standardized interface for Earth Observation (EO) analytics, enabling workflows to be executed across different computational backends. Although openEO supports multiple client languages, integrating R-based analytical methods in cloud environments remains limited. Existing solutions, such as OpenEOcubes, offer partial support but do not provide a general mechanism for exposing the broader range of geospatial, statistical, and machine learning tools available in R as openEO processes. This paper presents OpenEOcraft, a framework that integrates R-based EO workflows into the openEO ecosystem through a three-layer design comprising an execution engine, a process translation layer, and a RESTful API. The framework allows analytical functions from established R libraries to be made available as openEO-compliant processes with limited development effort. Two use cases illustrate its capabilities: time-series-based land cover classification and machine learning model reuse supported by its metadata, both of which are reproducible across R, Python, and the openEO Web Editor. OpenEOcraft extends the range of R methods available in openEO and supports reproducible EO analytics across heterogeneous clients.

rows.title: RECLAIM: A globally scalable machine learning framework to predict reservoir sedimentation and capacity loss from satellite-based earth observations
rows.abstract: Most reservoirs remain poorly sampled of their actual capacity due to the high costs and logistical demands of conventional sedimentation surveys. Here, we present RECLAIM (Reservoir Estimation of Capacity Loss using AI-based Methods), a globally scalable framework to predict absolute sedimentation rates using observed records and multi-decadal Earth observations from satellite data (1984-2023). Using a dataset of 1315 observations with 88 static and dynamic catchment, climatic, and reservoir-specific features, RECLAIM integrates gradient boosting models in a dynamic ensemble, achieving a prediction RMSE of 4.44 Million Cubic Meter (MCM)/year, MAE of 1.65 MCM/year, and R2 = 0.86 on the fixed test set. Cross-validation across 10 data partitions yields RMSE = 7.62 ± 4.86 MCM/year and MAE = 3.13 ± 1.66 MCM/year, confirming stable generalization across diverse sedimentation regimes. The development of RECLAIM revealed that absolute sedimentation rate is a more robust predictand than the widely used capacity loss rate, which loses sedimentation physics when normalized by reservoir capacity. The use of RECLAIM is expected to support the long-term sustainability of reservoir infrastructure globally.

rows.title: Software tooling support for atmospheric dispersion modeling of the AERMOD system
rows.abstract: Air pollution is a risk to public health. Identifying emission origins requires inventoried data to support air quality assessment. Then, simulations can be performed using the AERMOD system, recommended by the U.S. EPA. However, preparing the AERMOD input files is complex and error-prone because the data comes from multiple sources and must be in specific formats (e.g., SAM files). Since the available free tools have limitations and lack flexibility, users often rely on third-party services to obtain these files. This work presents AERMOD-IPT, an open-source tool that automates the generation of AERMOD input files. AERMOD-IPT was evaluated using BREEZEAERMOD/ISC and an emissions inventory from the Brazilian Institute of Environment and Renewable Natural Resources (IBAMA) for 2019–2021 in Toledo, Paraná, Brazil, including particulate matter (PM10), carbon monoxide (CO), and nitrogen oxides (NOx). Results show high reliability, supported by contour-map agreement and a Kappa index (k > 0.97).

rows.title: Improving groundwater level prediction based on optimized deep learning model with Coati algorithm
rows.abstract: Accurate groundwater level (GWL) estimation is of great significance to attain integrated water resources management and sustainable development goals. Recently, in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), nature-inspired optimization has been implemented in hydrology for training (calibration) of both statistical and process-based models. The presented study investigates the predictive performance of a hybrid deep learning technique, namely Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), with Coati Optimization Algorithm (COA) (CNN-COA hybridized model) in GWL modeling. Outcomes of CNN-COA are compared with improved CNN-HHO (Harris Hawks Optimization), Support Vector Regression (SVR) hybridized with COA and HHO (SVR-COA, SVR-HHO), and standalone CNN and SVR for GWL estimation. Evaluation statistics such as Nash-Sutcliffe efficiency (NSE), determination coefficient (R2), Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE) were used to assess the model's accuracy. The results show that the CNN-COA achieves greater accuracy than the other methods due to its effective exploration of the search space, avoiding local minima. In particular, among the three algorithms, the CNN-COA offered the best accuracy for all observation wells, with best results in Patyale Chak (NSE: 0.9932, MAE: 0.0468, R2: 0.9953, and RMSE: 0.0978) and worst in Badsoo (NSE: 0.9923, MAE: 1.0051, R2: 0.9945, and RMSE: 1.0517). Outcomes demonstrate substantial enhancement in prediction accuracy, highlighting the efficiency of the proposed methodology for GWL prediction.

rows.title: Geostatistical active learning for expanding monitoring networks for environmental decision-making: The case of groundwater nitrate
rows.abstract: Expanding environmental monitoring networks is a spatial sampling problem often addressed with pointwise uncertainty heuristics that ignore the neighborhood impact of new sites and the decision tasks motivating monitoring. We recast network densification as active learning and propose model-agnostic acquisition criteria, including a decision-aligned focal logit utility that prioritizes neighborhoods whose exceedance probabilities lie near regulatory thresholds. A look-ahead criterion based on the expected drop in prediction standard error (SE) is also examined. In a groundwater nitrate case study, the focal logit criterion consistently selected more informative sites than dispersion or SE heuristics, yielding up to 58 % greater gains in exceedance-mapping accuracy (Cohen’s κ). Focal logit and SE criteria outperformed pointwise counterparts by ∼45 % on average, while the look-ahead criterion performed well at much higher computational cost. The framework is simple, generalizable to other pollutants, and supports transparent, decision-oriented monitoring design.

rows.title: Modelling marine sand extraction pit evolution: Exploring design parameter sensitivity and cohesive sediment effects
rows.abstract: Marine sand extraction increases, calling for insight into the morphodynamic evolution of extraction pits and other bed forms, such as sand waves. We developed a quick, idealized, process-based numerical model to (1) simulate pit evolution; (2) quantify sensitivity to pit design parameters; (3) investigate interactions with cohesive sediment; and (4) explore sensitivity to pit location on the Netherlands Continental Shelf. In line with observations, results show how extraction pits either fill in or trigger sand wave formation within and around the pit. The cross-stream pit size primarily controls the extent of sand wave formation. Strikingly, the perturbed area relative to pit area decreases for larger pits. Cohesive sediment slows morphodynamic evolution and accumulates within the pit. Pit location influences the evolution trough local sediment properties and hydrodynamic conditions. Despite being limited to the initial morphodynamic response, the low computational cost enables extensive exploration of the parameter space.

rows.title: Enhancing groundwater representation in SWAT+gwflow with an open-source zonal parameterization and calibration workflow in R
rows.abstract: Modeling tools are essential to simulate groundwater-dominated catchments, yet hydrological models such as SWAT + often oversimplify groundwater processes, limiting their performance in hydrogeologically complex systems. This study presents a reproducible R-based workflow for the distributed parametrization and zonal calibration of the gwflow module in SWAT+, improving the representation of surface-groundwater interactions. Two alternative hydrogeological zoning approaches, based on lithology and permeability contrasts, were evaluated in the Tagus River headwaters. Calibration used daily performance metrics, groundwater contribution indices, and monthly reservoir inflows. Both approaches produced robust simulations, but the more detailed zoning yielded improved statistical performance and a slightly better representation of groundwater contribution to streamflow. The results demonstrate the added value of applying zonal calibration of the SWAT + model in conjunction with the gwflow module. The proposed methodology is freely available and transferable, enhancing the applicability of SWAT+ in hydrogeologically heterogeneous basins.

rows.title: Flow in float: Memory-efficient upstream flow length parallel computation using an IEEE-754-based union encoding
rows.abstract: Upstream flow length is a fundamental hydrologic parameter used in watershed characterization and environmental modeling. Continental-scale computation is increasingly constrained by memory usage under parallel execution. This study introduces the Memory-Efficient Upstream Flow Length algorithm and evaluates its variants under OpenMP shared-memory parallelism. We compare an explicit variant that stores upstream information separately with an in-place variant that stores the same information in a union data structure. Performance is evaluated across continental-, state-, and county-scale flow-direction datasets using up to 24 threads, with repeated runs. At the 30m Contiguous United States scale, results show that the explicit variant achieves 17.9% faster computation times at the cost of increased maximum resident set size, whereas the in-place variant reduces the memory footprint by 15.5% while exhibiting comparable or better scalability at higher thread counts. These findings highlight algorithmic properties that support scalable and memory-efficient upstream flow-length computation for large-scale hydrologic analysis.

rows.title: A graph-based approach for modeling landscape connectivity and analyzing runoff potential
rows.abstract: We present an open-source Python pipeline to automate landscape modeling for hydrological analysis, addressing the limitations of manual GIS processing.
