The proposed reproducible GIS-to-graph workflow transforms geospatial land-use data into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to map functional connectivity. The core contribution integrates three sequential phases: data cleaning, structural consolidation of patch-boundary attributes, and topological generation. Nodes represent discrete soil patches, while directed edges represent topographic boundaries oriented by gravitational potential. The framework implements spatial graph algorithms—including degree centrality, Breadth-First Search, and an adapted Bellman–Ford procedure to identify potential runoff source areas and critical connectivity corridors within the model’s topological assumptions. Edges are weighted using a composite metric integrating elevation difference, land-cover contrast, and boundary length. A case study involving 1427 patches demonstrates high computational efficiency with O(|V|+|E|) complexity for path identification. This scalable software solution bridges computer science methodology and geoscientific applications, providing a robust tool for precision environmental management and runoff mitigation planning.

rows.title: A physics-informed predictive control framework for joint regulation of water level and velocity in open channels
rows.abstract: Traditional regulation of open-channel flow has primarily emphasized water levels, although flow velocity is equally important for sediment transport and aquatic environments. To enable real-time regulation of both variables, this study proposes a physics-informed predictive control framework that integrates hydrodynamic principles with data-driven learning for real-time multi-variable regulation. A control-embedded physics-informed neural networks framework is developed for rapid and physically consistent prediction of hydrodynamic states, and is coupled with model predictive control for efficient constrained optimization. HEC-RAS is adopted for accurate state initialization. Numerical results show that the proposed model achieves higher prediction accuracy than purely data-driven surrogates, particularly in data-scarce cases, while realizing coordinated water-level tracking, avoiding low-velocity stagnation, and substantially reducing online computational cost. The framework provides insights into the development of efficient, physics-informed predictive control strategies for real-time multi-variable regulation of open-channel and riverine flow systems.

rows.title: Enhancement of hydrological time series prediction with Real-World Time Series Generative Adversarial Network-based synthetic data and deep learning models
rows.abstract: Accurate river water quality forecasting is essential for environmental and public health. However it is challenging due to limited high-resolution data. To overcome this, a comprehensive framework for data augmentation and forecasting is developed. The proposed approach leverages available flow and water temperature (WT) measurements alongside sparse dissolved oxygen (DO) observations to enhance the temporal resolution of the dataset and employ Real-World Time Series Generative Adversarial Network (RTSGAN) to create additional synthetic dataset that retain real-world data characteristics. Both the original and synthetic data are then used to train two deep learning models, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and Long Short-Term Memory networks (LSTMs), which predict DO and WT at three hydrological stations three days ahead. The results indicate that GNNs, through the combined use of synthetic data and spatial dependencies, achieve up to 43.4% higher accuracy at upstream locations, whereas LSTMs improve predictive performance by up to 15%.

rows.title: HydroBlox: AI-assisted visual programming framework for enhanced scientific reproducibility in hydrology
rows.abstract: Scientific workflow reproducibility for hydrological and environmental analyses remains a challenge due to the heterogeneity of data sources, analysis protocols, and evolving visualization needs. This study introduces HydroBlox, a client-side browser-based framework that supports the creation, execution, and export of hydrological workflows using a visual programming interface. The platform integrates modular web libraries to perform data retrieval, statistical analysis, and visualization directly in the browser. Two case studies are presented to demonstrate the platform: precipitation–streamflow response analysis in the Iowa River Basin and SPI-based drought characterization using a workflow that produces ensemble drought scenarios. Results demonstrate the system's capacity to facilitate reproducible, portable, and extensible hydrological analyses across a range of spatial and temporal scales. The study discusses the architecture, implementation, and capabilities of the system and explores its implications for collaborative research, education, and low-code scientific computing in hydrology.

rows.title: CausalHMoE-STFNN: A two-stage causal-inspired spatio-temporal model for multi-pollutant air quality inference
rows.abstract: Real-time air quality monitoring is crucial for pollution control and public health, yet sparse station distribution limits spatial coverage. Existing deep learning models typically focus on single pollutants and fail to jointly capture spatiotemporal continuity, local heterogeneity, and causal mechanisms. To address this, we propose CausalHMoE-STFNN, a two-stage multi-pollutant causal inference model. Stage I builds a Causal Encoder with Hybrid Mixture of Experts (CausalHMoE), where a Causal Encoder models causal relations between local features and pollutants, and a Hybrid Mixture of Experts captures inter-pollutant interactions for multi-task initial prediction. Stage II employs a short-term Spatio-Temporal Field Neural Network (STFNN) to model the continuous evolution of air quality and refine inference using Stage I outputs. Experiments conducted on the Chongqing and Beijing datasets demonstrate that the proposed model achieves the best or near-best performance across most pollutants and evaluation metrics. Compared with the strongest baseline model, CausalHMoE-STFNN reduces the Overall RMSE by 10.18% and 21.86% on the Chongqing and Beijing datasets, respectively, while the Overall MAE is reduced by 13.08% and 8.14%, confirming its accuracy, component effectiveness, and interpretability.

rows.title: Anomaly detection using continuous wavelet transforms and local active information storage scores: An application to water distribution networks
rows.abstract: The identification of anomalies within time series is a mature field. This paper, however, introduces a distinct methodology tailored for detecting extremely subtle anomalies in data heavily corrupted by significant noise and trends originating from non-polynomial and nonlinear dynamics. Our innovative technique utilizes a tailored Continuous Wavelet Transform (CWT) based filtering pipeline to deconstruct data and effectively remove nonlinear and non-polynomial trends, subsequently leading to precise identification of anomalies using Local Active Information Storage (LAIS) as an unsupervised anomaly indicator. Our analysis of the LAIS scores makes it possible to detect anomalies. More specifically, this kind of analysis, when applied to steady pressures inside a Water Distribution Network (WDN), allows us to identify very tiny incipient leaks. We successfully tested our method on publicly available realistic synthetic data, pertaining to Hanoi WDN, containing minute leaks that other forefront methods available in literature were unable to detect.

rows.title: Coupling SWAT+ with machine learning-enhanced ECMWF seasonal forecasts for predicting inflows to Entrepeñas and Buendía reservoirs
rows.abstract: The Segura River Basin in southeastern Spain relies on the Tagus–Segura water transfer for agricultural activities. Reliable one-to three-month and seasonal reservoir inflow forecasts are essential for managing transfers from the Upper Tagus River Basin reservoirs (Entrepeñas and Buendía). This study develops a seasonal hydrological forecasting framework using ECMWF's SEAS5 ensemble climate predictions. Bias-corrected forecasts with machine learning generate daily precipitation and temperatures up to seven months ahead. These drive a calibrated SWAT+ model to simulate reservoir inflows. Model calibration (2000-2009) and validation (2010-2019) showed strong performance (NSE >0.7, PBIAS <14%). Bias-corrected forecasts enabled skilful inflow predictions, with high reliability at 1–3 months (NSE = 0.91–0.73) and seasonal scales. Performance declines toward 7 months (NSE = 0.58), although CRPSS remains generally positive, outperforming traditional estimates calculated from historical data. This demonstrates the value of integrating seasonal climate forecasts into operational water-resource decision-making in drought-prone basins.

rows.title: Physically consistent dynamic graph learning for multi-horizon nutrient prediction in a gate-controlled river network
rows.abstract: Regulated river networks exhibit strongly nonstationary nutrient dynamics driven by time-varying hydrologic connectivity and gate operations, which challenges stable multi-horizon forecasting of Total Nitrogen (TN) and Total Phosphorus (TP). We develop the Dynamic Edge Weight and Virtual-node Spatio-Temporal Multi-Variable Gate-control Graph Neural Network (DEWV-STMV-G), a control-aware spatiotemporal graph learning framework for nutrient prediction in gate-regulated river networks. The model integrates node-wise sequential encoding for short-term hydrology–water-quality memory, basin-scale meteorology–calendar encoding for exogenous forcing and periodicity, and explicit gate-control conditioning to represent operation-dependent regime shifts. The river system is represented as a transport-consistent dynamic directed weighted graph, where edge directions follow instantaneous flow signs and edge weights vary with transport intensity and distance decay. To preserve topological closure under sparse monitoring, unobserved confluences are completed through virtual-node estimation before graph propagation. DEWV-STMV-G directly predicts TN and TP at 3, 6, 12, and 24 h horizons without recursive rollout. Using hourly observations from August 1, 2023 to September 22, 2025 and a time-ordered 80/20 train–test split, DEWV-STMV-G achieved robust multi-horizon prediction performance. On the test set, TN R2 decreased from 0.9665 at 3 h to 0.9035 at 24 h, while TP R2 decreased from 0.9665 to 0.8328, with MAE and RMSE increasing as lead time grew. The model outperformed representative spatiotemporal graph baselines and ablated variants, demonstrating the value of jointly modeling dynamic connectivity, virtual-node completion, exogenous drivers, and regulation-aware conditioning. Stratified evaluation showed that gate-opening periods were the main source of long-horizon uncertainty, whereas steady periods retained high predictive skill at 24 h. External validation in an independent regulated river network further showed averaged R2 values of 0.8250 for TN and 0.8725 for TP, providing preliminary evidence of cross-basin transferability. These results suggest that DEWV-STMV-G can support short-term forecasting and early-warning applications in regulated river-network water-quality management.

rows.title: A novel approach for retrieving water use efficiency and gross primary production from the “analytical triangle” technique: extending the Ts/VI feature space properties
rows.abstract: Monitoring and quantifying the carbon-water exchange under climate change is a key indicator for the study of interactions between carbon and water cycles in terrestrial ecosystems. To support the growing need for monitoring surface–atmosphere exchange processes, the present study proposes a novel methodological framework for deriving carbon components from the Ts/VI feature space, coupled with land process-based modelling, which can be applied across local, regional, and large spatial scales using EO data. The current framework, introduces a proof-of-concept for a new scheme that extends the application of the “analytical triangle”, by producing spatially explicit, instantaneous maps of ambient gross primary productivity, carbon concentration, and water use efficiency. An initial evaluation of the proof-of-concept methodological framework was tested in 6 sites belong to the global network of ground measurements FLUXNET, across 5 different ecosystem types, for a total of 35 days, using the Landsat-8 EO data coupled with the SimSphere model. Results of GPP and WUE produced a small bias of −0.103 μmol CO2 m−2 s−1 and RMSD of 7.66 μmol CO2 m−2 s−1 and also a bias of 2.216 kg m−3 and RMSD of 4.54 kg m−3, respectively. The predicted [CO2] showed high deviation (bias of −18.24 μmol mol−1), and a moderate overall agreement (R = 0.52). The predictions have shown a reasonable level of agreement with FLUXNET observations, providing a preliminary proof of concept for the proposed method, with potential for future applications at regional to large scales. Yet, further investigation is ongoing to confirm its to access the method's generality and its ability to represent physical processes across various ecosystems.

rows.title: A potentially transferable grid-based SWAT+ framework for groundwater recharge estimation informed by satellite-derived evapotranspiration in data-scarce volcanic islands
rows.abstract: Quantifying groundwater recharge in data-scarce volcanic islands is essential for sustainable water management, yet challenged by limited monitoring networks and the lack of perennial surface water bodies. This study introduces a potentially transferable grid-based SWAT + framework, an innovative adaptation of semi-distributed hydrological modeling, to better capture spatiotemporal hydrogeological and climatic heterogeneity in such environments. The framework integrates satellite-derived evapotranspiration for physically consistent parameterization, employing Sobol global sensitivity analysis followed by a two-stage calibration (hydrological ratios and remote sensing-based). Demonstrated on El Hierro (Canary Islands) as a representative case, the model uncovers significant recharge variability influenced predominantly by land use, with secondary controls from soil and topography, yielding mean annual recharge of 58 mm yr−1 (P05–P95: 31–89 mm yr−1), substantially lower than prior local assessments. By leveraging remote sensing and advanced calibration, this approach enhances accuracy in semi-arid volcanic settings and is potentially applicable to other semi-arid volcanic contexts, enabling resilient water resource planning amid climate change uncertainties.

rows.title: Automating shoreline extraction from beach imaging systems for coastal monitoring
rows.abstract: High-frequency coastal monitoring is essential for understanding shoreline dynamics under climate change and supporting coastal adaptation. Although ground-based remote sensing offers a scalable solution for data acquisition, automated shoreline extraction from beach imaging systems remains challenging due to variable image quality, complex geometries, and environmental conditions. This study presents a robust deep learning framework for instantaneous shoreline extraction from crowd-sourced imagery (i.e., smartphone captures). We benchmarked state-of-the-art segmentation models against a traditional histogram-based deterministic method. Results show that convolutional neural network approaches, particularly DeepLabV3 with 512 ×512 patches, significantly outperform conventional methods, achieving spatial reliability comparable to manual digitisation. Importantly, the model overcomes perspective distortion and interpolation artefacts in rectified imagery across diverse tidal environments, showing strong environmental robustness despite site diversity and data imbalance. The framework has been deployed as an open-source, containerised module within the European Open Science Cloud, enabling transferable and operational image-based coastline monitoring.

rows.title: SurtGIS: A high-performance raster geospatial analysis library in Rust with WebAssembly and Python support
rows.abstract: We present SurtGIS, an open-source raster geospatial analysis library in Rust providing 127 terrain, hydrological, and remote sensing algorithms. The library compiles to native code with automatic parallelization via Rayon, to WebAssembly for browser-based applications, and exposes Python bindings through PyO3. Key contributions include Florinsky’s complete 14-curvature morphometric system, three depression handling algorithms, and four flow direction methods. Benchmarks on synthetic DEMs up to 20,0002 cells demonstrate speedups on full GeoTIFF pipelines: 1.7–1.8× over GDAL and 4.5–4.9× over GRASS GIS for slope; 2.0× over GDAL for aspect; and 7.5–23.1× for D8 flow accumulation. WebAssembly adds 10–32× overhead versus native Rust but enables browser-based terrain analysis unavailable in existing tools. Numerical accuracy is within 5.7×10−5 degrees RMSE against analytical solutions.

rows.title: Improving precipitation forecasts through machine learning of the decomposed high- and low-frequency components
rows.abstract: Traditional forecasting models decompose time series into multiple subseries but typically simulate all components using a single modeling approach. In this study, we proposed a novel methodology to disaggregate precipitation time series into distinct high- and low-frequency components and simulate them separately for different climates. We tested the proposed method on monthly and annual precipitation, representing arid, semi-arid, and humid climates in Iran. The proposed approach demonstrated superior performance compared to single model approaches. Implementing separate modeling of the components improved forecast accuracy by 39–44%. A climate-specific analysis revealed distinct performance patterns. Arid climate stations achieved high precision scores (precision = 0.83), while semi-arid stations showed a moderate accuracy (precision = 0.495). Humid climate stations maintained robust performance (precision = 0.74). The proposed two-step temporal decomposition approach can effectively address the non-stationary and random characteristics of precipitation time series, thereby improving forecast accuracy.

rows.title: A tightly coupled socio-hydrological model with feedback pathways for water availability assessment: A case study of the Weihe River Basin
rows.abstract: The interactions between socio-economic and water resources subsystems are increasingly significant under climate change and intense human activities. Research on the evolution of future water systems is essential to understand regional water sustainability. However, traditional socio-hydrological systems normally focus on the response of the water resources system to external disturbances, while the factors of water resources availability on socio-economic development are represented in a limited way. In this paper, a novel socio-hydrological model, constructed by coupling a distributed hydrological model and a system dynamics model, has been proposed. The coupled models simulate dynamic feedbacks between socio-economic and water resources systems. Specifically, increasing water stress triggers five negative feedback pathways that limit social-economic development, and lower the water supply-demand rodio, thereby reducing social water demand. Through a case study of the Weihe River Basin in China, where the model achieved an NSE of 0.9 for streamflow during the validation period, results reveal that industrial production is more sensitive to changes in water resources than population and irrigation. Future water availability can be overestimated (up to 3%) if neglecting the influence of socio-economic development on water resources; while ignoring the impact of water resources on socio-economic development can lead to an underestimation of water availability by 7.8%. The model provides an online tool for coupled system simulation and offers insights into system feedbacks and coevolution under climate change and socioeconomic development.

rows.title: A self-supervised deep learning method for retrieving historically similar extreme rainfall patterns
rows.abstract: Deciphering current extreme rainfall patterns through the retrieval of historical counterparts supports contextual rainfall assessment and hydrometeorological modelling. However, existing methods still struggle to capture the pronounced temporal variability and irregular spatial organization of extreme rainfall patterns, and their limited scalability hinders adaptation to growing rainfall archives. This study proposes a novel method for rainfall analog retrieval at hourly, daily, and event scales, integrating a vision transformer with masked pretraining to learn rainfall representations, an intensity-guided loss to embed hydrologic priors and emphasize extremes, and a spatiotemporal evaluation system for rainfall event evolution. Experiments demonstrate accurate and efficient retrieval of diverse rainfall patterns, with a mean query time of 21.35 ms over more than 10000 rainfall maps. The label-free method scales to expanding rainfall archives and retrieves dynamic analogues for localized extremes and rare large-scale events, extending retrieval from static pattern matching to dynamic event tracking.

rows.title: A generic aggregate reservoir module with a storage capacity curve for enhancing lumped hydrological models in human-modified basins
rows.abstract: To enhance the flood simulation accuracy of the Xin'anjiang (XAJ) model, an improved Xin'anjiang model (I-XAJ) was developed by incorporating an aggregated reservoir module with storage and discharge functions into the original framework. Remote sensing technology was employed to extract information on water storage structures within the basin. In the aggregated reservoir module, a storage capacity curve was established to analyze the retention effects caused by the non-uniform spatial distribution of small water storage bodies, and outflow was calculated using the weir-flow formula for ungated spillways. To evaluate the forecasting accuracy of the I-XAJ model, thirty-one flood events were selected from the Huangnizhuang (HNZ) basin. Compared with the XAJ model, simulation accuracy of floods was significantly improved by the IXAJ model through consideration of small water bodies within the basin. The model performance for flood peaks was increased by 44.5 percentage points in the calibration period and 25 percentage points in the validation period.

rows.title: EVAonline: An open-source web platform for global reference evapotranspiration estimation via multi-source data fusion
rows.abstract: Accurate modeling of reference evapotranspiration (ET0) is critical for environmental management but is hindered by input uncertainties and data scarcity in emerging agricultural frontiers. We introduce EVAonline, a new open-source, scalable web platform providing robust ET0 estimation via multi-source data fusion. Built on a modular hexagonal architecture integrating six meteorological APIs, the software implements an adaptive Kalman filter constrained by 30-year climatological priors to harmonize disparate datasets. Validated in Brazil’s MATOPIBA region across 17 sites (186,286 observations), the framework achieved a Kling-Gupta Efficiency of 0.814. The fusion process significantly mitigated uncertainty, reducing Mean Absolute Error by 50% and systematic bias by 95% compared to individual products. By resolving hydroclimatic modeling challenges in data-scarce regions through software engineering, EVAonline delivers a scalable, open-source decision-support architecture designed for global deployment; its quantitative validation here is restricted to the MATOPIBA region against BR–DWGD, with broader multi-climate and forecast-horizon validation left for future work.

rows.title: Water–food–energy nexus pathways in the Nile river basin under climate change uncertainty
rows.abstract: Managing the Water, Food and Energy (WFE) nexus in transboundary rivers like the Nile is challenging due to inter-sectoral complexity, socio-economic developments and uncertain future climate conditions. We assess the long-term WFE impacts under a changing climate by employing an integrated System Dynamics model for the Nile basin. Our results suggest that climate change impacts may exceed those of planned infrastructure alone. Under Representative Concentration Pathway (RCP) 4.5, average annual river discharges will reduce by 8%, while under RCP 8.5, the range varies between −39% and +30%. Importantly, improved agricultural productivity could mitigate climate change impacts, increasing basin-wide food production by over 60%. Planned hydropower projects, projected to add 35 ± 4.1 TWh/year without considering climate change, may vary by +24% to −40% under climate change scenarios. Cooperative implementation of the WFE nexus approach presents an opportunity to reduce regional conflicts and improve resource sustainability through mutually beneficial policies and solutions.

rows.title: A diagnostic framework for interpreting spatiotemporal probabilistic forecasts
rows.abstract: Aggregate probabilistic scores are central to evaluating forecast quality but often obscure spatiotemporal variability in uncertainty. We propose a diagnostic framework for spatiotemporal probabilistic forecasts that complements standard metrics with a visual grammar linking geographic maps and polar representations. Spatial order is fixed, diagnostic magnitude encoded radially, and forecast horizons shown as concentric rings, enabling joint assessment of interval width, interval exceedance, horizon-dependent drift, and quantile structure. We apply the framework to annual land-subsidence forecasts in Zhongshan, China, comparing the eXtreme Temporal Fusion Transformer (XTFT), Quantile Gradient Boosting Machine (QGBM), and Quantile Autoregression (QAR). Results show that XTFT is closest to nominal coverage with ordered quantiles, while QGBM and QAR exhibit under-coverage. Spatial diagnostics further reveal that similar median fields can mask substantial differences in uncertainty geometry, interval exceedance, and distributional spread. The model-agnostic framework supports interpretation, comparison, and monitoring of spatial probabilistic forecasts.

rows.title: From theory to practice. A shiny R app for climate-smart forestry assessment
rows.abstract: Climate-Smart Forestry (CSF) integrates mitigation, adaptation, and socio-economic performance to address climate change in forest management. Despite the increasing use of CSF indicators, a standardized and user-friendly operational tool is still lacking. This study presents the Climate-Smart Forestry Assessment Tool (CSF-AT), a web-based application that automates the calculation of a composite climate-smart index, integrates the three CSF pillars, and generates visual outputs to support research and management decisions. The tool's usability and versatility are demonstrated through two case studies. In the Collemeluccio Forest (Italy), CSF-AT highlights the climate-smartness implications of alternative silvicultural strategies and supports scenario exploration. A second application, using ICP Forests Level II data from Scots pine stands across five European countries, reveals spatial and temporal patterns and enables cross-country comparisons. Results confirm the tool's applicability across scales, offering a transparent, standardized, and accessible platform that bridges the gap between CSF conceptual frameworks and its practical implementation.

rows.title: Editorial Board
Bias-corrected exceedance mapping of groundwater nitrate using geostatistical and machine-learning models
rows.abstract: Spatial models used in environmental assessment are often used to predict concentrations, even when the underlying decision problem concerns the delineation of threshold exceedance areas. We show that the common practice of thresholding point predictions can introduce substantial bias in estimated exceedance areas. We propose a decision-aligned modeling and evaluation workflow that frames exceedance mapping as a probabilistic prediction task. The approach calibrates exceedance maps to match an unbiased area estimate and assesses model performance using target-weighted cross-validation. In a groundwater-nitrate case study, several widely used interpolation and machine-learning models underestimate exceedance area by 80%–98% when exceedance areas are derived by thresholding concentration predictions, despite competitive concentration-based error metrics. Area calibration removes this bias and yields a balanced trade-off between omission and commission. The workflow is model-agnostic and compatible with standard geostatistical and machine-learning methods, providing a general framework for task-aligned modeling and uncertainty quantification in environmental applications involving threshold-based decisions.

rows.title: Towards precision irrigation scheduling from UAV-based observations: Model structure
rows.abstract: Using UAV-based near-surface observations for root-zone soil moisture (RZSM) estimation requires a model with at least two layers and minimal complexity while this design has been overlooked. To address this limitation, a series of soil moisture models, from two-layer to multi-layer configurations were developed. Key processes, including vertical soil moisture redistribution, evapotranspiration, drainage, and infiltration, were progressively refined and systematically evaluated. A two-layer model incorporating Buckingham Darcy based vertical fluxes and a water stress adjusted evapotranspiration scheme (R-FLX-ET) was identified as the optimal configuration, achieving high accuracy with limited complexity. The R-FLX-ET model produced NSE up to 0.92 for RZSM and 0.81 for near surface soil moisture at hourly resolution, with RMSE below 0.03 cm3 cm−3, outperforming both the single-layer model and Aqua Crop. Model robustness was confirmed through numerical stability analysis and validation across four monitoring stations. R-FLX-ET offers a computationally efficient framework suitable for UAV-assisted precision irrigation applications.

rows.title: A review of how uncertainties are assessed in water quality modeling: A paradigm shift towards more complete practices
rows.abstract: Water quality modeling (WQM) faces enormous uncertainties due principally to process complexity representation and data limitations. Its uncertainties can never be entirely eliminated but can be managed by an uncertainty assessment (UA) approach that enhances confidence in both modeling process decisions and its outcomes. A paradigm shift from uncertainty analysis of a model to broader UA is vital for testing assumptions and evaluating model reliability from multiple methods, assumptions and perspectives. Reviewing the past decade of WQM papers reveals that attention to uncertainty is not routine. When it occurs, coverage of uncertainty is strongest for traditional sources: data, parametric and structural. We recommend broader integration of methods, including scaling comparisons, cross-validation, graphical and statistical performance evaluation, scenario analysis of non-probabilistic assumptions, explanation of choices, documentation to record assumptions and model evaluation exercises, and improved communication with interest groups. Progress also depends on computational efficiencies to explore assumptions more completely.

rows.title: Coupling process-based models with machine learning for the prediction of soil carbon and nitrogen cycling
rows.abstract: Accurate prediction of soil carbon (C) and nitrogen (N) cycling is essential for understanding ecosystem functioning, supporting sustainable agriculture, and mitigating climate change. This review summarizes recent progress in predicting soil C–N dynamics, contrasting the mechanistic fidelity yet parametric rigidity of process-based models against the predictive accuracy but limited extrapolative capacity of machine learning (ML). We synthesize specific coupling strategies, from ML-driven parameter optimization and surrogate emulation to physics-informed neural networks, highlighting their potential to improve predictive skill, scalability, and interpretability. Persistent challenges include spatial scale mismatches, increasing computational demands, and the critical need to disentangle multi-dimensional uncertainties (e.g., input, structural, and prediction errors) for large-scale applications. Finally, we outline emerging pathways, particularly the integration of multi-scale remote and proximal sensing and edge-AI frameworks, advocating an interdisciplinary research ecosystem to enable more accurate and actionable predictions of soil C–N dynamics, informing sustainable land management and food security worldwide.

rows.title: Dynamic canopy initiation in SWAT-C: Integrating climate-driven phenology and MODIS LAI in data-limited regions
rows.abstract: The present study improves the forest growth dynamics in the SWAT-C model for data limited tropical regions through dynamic initiation of the canopy growth cycle using the climate driven triggers. The improvement in the model was achieved by two approaches: (i) improving the parameters of the model obtained from MODIS LAI (M2) and (ii) through modification of source code (M3). The performance of both the modified models and default model (M1) was similar (NSE, KGE >0.75) for streamflow simulation. However, the improved models performed well in simulating ET, when compared against MODIST ET, with M2 and M3 reporting 19% and 21% lower bias than M1 in forested sub-basins. Similarly, the simulations of sediment yield and carbon storage dynamics varied in the three models. The study demonstrates the implication of these variations in management of natural resources, emphasizing the need for improving the forest growth dynamics.

rows.title: DarcyWarp: A graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated multigrid solver for repeated 2D fixed-transmissivity groundwater solves validated against reference solvers
rows.abstract: Repeated steady-state groundwater solves for calibration and uncertainty analysis are often limited by runtime. We present DarcyWarp, a graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated geometric multigrid solver for two-dimensional, steady-state, single-layer groundwater flow using a fixed-transmissivity formulation on structured grids. DarcyWarp implements an explicit cell-integrated five-point finite-difference operator and multigrid cycle as Python kernels just in time compiled for GPU execution with NVIDIA Warp, and supports areal source/sink terms, prescribed head, no-flow, and general-head boundaries. Validation against a sparse finite-difference direct solve and MODFLOW 6 on matched grids shows close head agreement, consistent residuals, and mass-balance closure. Benchmarks span matched-grid single-instance cases from 104 to 9×106 active cells and two 48-case repeated-solve ensembles. DarcyWarp reaches about 70 times end-to-end speedup over MODFLOW 6 in the single-instance suite and order-of-magnitude throughput gains in ensembles, enabling reproducible repeated-solve workflows on commodity GPUs.

rows.title: A comparative study of deep learning and process-based models for hourly flood simulation under a unified input and optimization framework
rows.abstract: Hourly flood forecasting is critical for disaster mitigation, yet methodological inconsistencies in input architectures and optimization algorithms often undermine comparisons between Process-Based Models (PBMs) and Deep Learning Models (DLMs). This study presents a systematic evaluation framework that standardizes these elements to ensure an equitable comparison of PBM and DLM in hourly flood simulation. We established a comparative framework incorporating four representative models: the Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) for DLMs, alongside the HBV and Tank models for PBMs. Applied across seven Chinese catchments, our investigation yielded principal findings: (1) The GRU model, when fed with the complete flood process as input, achieved superior simulation accuracy compared to using sliding-window samples; (2) Adam is an effective method for parameter calibration within PBMs; (3) Under unified input and optimization conditions, DLMs generally achieved superior simulation performance to PBMs across most catchments.

rows.title: Global structure-aware R-Tree: a spatial indexing mechanism using deep reinforcement learning and self-play
rows.abstract: R- Trees and R-Tree variants have been widely adopted as the spatial indexing structures in the underlying databases of major Geographic Information Systems (GIS). However, most traditional R-Tree variants rely on handcrafted heuristic rules or parameters derived from expert knowledge, often facing performance limitations with locally optimal structures. In this paper, we introduce the Global Structure-Aware R-Tree (GSAR-Tree), an approach for constructing an R-Tree variant using deep reinforcement learning (DRL) with a self-play mechanism. Our approach replaces the traditional heuristic rules with the RL agent's choices, yielding more informed and globally optimized insertion decisions. We performed a series of experiments leveraging multiple synthetic datasets with varying distributions alongside real-world OpenStreetMap (OSM) data, and evaluated query efficiency under different data volumes, training-set ratios, and query sizes. Experimental results show that our proposed GSAR-Tree outperforms R∗-Tree, achieving a reduction in node accesses ranging from 37.9% to 1193.8%.

rows.title: Estimation of lake storage volumes in the Lagan River catchment in southern Sweden using a modified version of the Australian Water Resources Assessment–Landscape model (AWRA-L)
rows.abstract: In an era of global change, understanding available water resources is increasingly important. In Sweden, this challenge has intensified due to climate change driven pressures and rising water demand, yet suitable tools for assessing water storage remain limited. This study presents a novel approach for evaluating surface water storage using a modified Australian Water Resources Assessment Landscape model (AWRA-L). Physics-informed rating curves were incorporated during model optimization and tested over a five-year period (2018–2022) in a case study of three lakes in the Lagan River catchment, southwest Sweden. Results show that the modified model reproduces seasonal storage dynamics well, with average R2, NSE, and KGE′ values of 0.70, 0.68, and 0.71, respectively. Our findings suggest the approach has strong potential for accurately assessing surface storage dynamics and demonstrate that, with appropriate adaptation, the AWRA-L model is applicable outside Australia, offering an improved tool for evaluating lake storage volumes.

rows.title: Multivariate SWAT streamflow and surface water storage calibration enables upper Mississippi River Basin wetland change scenarios
rows.abstract: Surface water storage (e.g., wetlands, lakes) is not typically considered in hydrological model calibrations. We tested a multivariate calibration process, incorporating Sentinel-1 and -2 surface water storage, for a Soil and Water Assessment Tool model across the 0.5 million km2 Upper Mississippi River Basin. While 19% of the 2000 parameter sets adequately simulated discharge (Kling-Gupta efficiency >0.5), only 5% also adequately simulated surface water storage (mean absolute error <2 m), reducing model output uncertainty. Using the best calibrated model, we found that changes in surface water storage capacity most strongly affected discharge during the first annual peak flow (i.e., floods), when storage was filling. Increases in upstream surface water storage capacity resulted in projected decreases in peak flow and flashiness, with changes persisting downstream to the watershed outlet. Our findings demonstrate the importance of surface water storage in multivariate model calibration processes to inform river discharge and flood impact predictions.

rows.title: Downscaling neural network for coastal simulations
rows.abstract: Learning the fine-scale details of a coastal ocean simulation from a coarse representation is a challenging task. For real-world applications, high-resolution simulations are necessary to advance understanding of many coastal processes, specifically, to predict flooding resulting from tsunamis and storm surges. We propose a Downscaling Neural Network for Coastal Simulation (DNNCS) for spatiotemporal enhancement to learn the high-resolution numerical solution. Given images of coastal simulations produced on low-resolution computational meshes using low polynomial order discontinuous Galerkin discretizations and a coarse temporal resolution, the proposed DNNCS learns to produce high-resolution free surface elevation and velocity visualizations in both time and space. To model the dynamic changes over time and space, we propose grid-aware spatiotemporal attention to project the temporal features to the spatial domain for non-local feature matching. The coordinate information is also utilized via positional encoding. For the final reconstruction, we use the spatiotemporal bilinear operation to interpolate the missing frames and then expand the feature maps to the frequency domain for residual mapping. Besides data-driven losses, the proposed physics-informed loss guarantees gradient consistency and momentum changes, leading to a 24% reduction in root-mean-square error compared to the model trained with only data-driven losses. Our DNNCS is trained on a coastal simulation dataset and uses it for model optimization and evaluation. Our method shows superior downscaling quality and fast computation compared to the state-of-the-art methods.

rows.title: A novel framework for quantifying threshold-controlled surface hydrologic connectivity in depression-dominated watersheds
rows.abstract: Surface hydrologic connectivity is an important hydrologic characteristic for understanding hydrologic processes and catchment responses in depression-dominated areas. While tremendous recent interest remains focused on surface depression-induced hydrologic connectivity, few studies have illustrated the progressive development of hydro-connectedness at the watershed scale. The objective of this study is to identify and quantify threshold-controlled hydrologic connectivity behaviors for depression-dominated watersheds. We present a novel depression-oriented hydro-connectedness (HCd) characterization framework to recognize spatial distribution and topographic parameters of surface depressions and channels as well as the associated static/dynamic connections. The HCd was effectively applied to a depression-dominated watershed in North Dakota, U.S., and its unique capability was emphasized by the comparisons with other depression-oriented characterization algorithms/tools. The results provide an advanced understanding of the progressive expansion of connected areas and contributing area of the watershed outlet. The findings deliver new insights into threshold-controlled hydrologic connectivity and overland flow dynamics in depression-dominated areas, thereby facilitating water resource management and flood risk assessment, and supporting the development of depression-oriented hydrologic models for improved runoff prediction.

rows.title: Development of an R package for probabilistic modeling of vapor intrusion based on the Johnson and Ettinger Model
rows.abstract: Vapor intrusion is a dynamic process at hazardous waste sites where volatile contaminants in contaminated soil or groundwater vaporize and migrate through the soil strata and along preferential pathways into buildings where people can potentially be exposed. The paucity of data and the presence of other indoor sources of contaminants make assessment of the public health implications from vapor intrusion challenging, often requiring modeling and monitoring to develop multiple lines of evidence. This article describes and demonstrates a novel R package, vapintr, ATSDR created to facilitate the use of U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's Johnson and Ettinger vapor intrusion model spreadsheet to allow the user to have the flexibility to evaluate multiple scenarios and enable stochastic simulation of multiple input parameters. This enables the user to understand the underlying sensitivity of the model to uncertain inputs. Additionally, vapintr aggregates and visualizes the inputs and outputs of the model alongside empirical site data and user supplied risk benchmarks and background values. Users can utilize the vapintr package using R code or through an interactive Shiny® application. To date, no R package has been created with the objective of facilitating evaluation of such sites using multiple lines of evidence. The vapintr package not only improves the efficiency of using the current Johnson and Ettinger Model spreadsheet but also provides enhancements in visualization, data management, and sensitivity analysis.

rows.title: Machine learning in urban stormwater management: A review
rows.abstract: Urban stormwater systems generate large and heterogeneous datasets from in-situ sensors, remote sensing, and distributed monitoring networks, yet conventional models often struggle with nonlinear dynamics, data gaps, and scalability. This study presents a structured synthesis of machine learning (ML) approaches for urban stormwater modeling, focusing on their ability to address these limitations. We organize the literature across four domains — water quality prediction, flow modeling, infrastructure management, and real-time control — and introduce an integrated framework linking sensing, prediction, assessment, and adaptive management. Across the reviewed literature, ML provides the greatest value where stormwater applications involve heterogeneous data, nonlinear system behavior, and adaptive decision support; however, reliable deployment remains constrained by both technical and operational barriers including transferability, uncertainty, scalability, and workflow integration. We identify future research needs centered on hybrid physics–ML modeling, benchmark datasets, uncertainty-aware AI, digital twins, and transferable modeling frameworks to support robust and operational stormwater decision-support systems.

rows.title: Is the 5 mm inflow-based subdivision method necessary in the Xinanjiang model?
rows.abstract: The Xinanjiang (XAJ) model is widely used and a de facto standard hydrological model in China. However, its implementation remains ambiguous due to the 5 mm inflow-based subdivision, originally introduced to control numerical errors in time discretization. Ambiguity persists regarding its necessity, scope, and threshold, leading to inconsistent implementations and hindering model reproducibility. To address this issue, we introduce a differential-form XAJ model and employ high-order numerical solvers to obtain a high-accuracy benchmark. Idealized experiment and large-sample applications are conducted to evaluate the subdivision method. Results show that subdivision is necessary for error control and should be applied across all modules. The 5 mm threshold is generally adequate, but smaller thresholds are required in a subset of watersheds. This study provides the first quantitative assessment of the subdivision method, resolves a long-standing ambiguity in the XAJ model, and highlights the importance of explicitly accounting for numerical implementation in hydrological modeling.

rows.title: BiGRU-dXAJ: A hybrid hydrologic model enabling differentiable parameter learning for runoff simulation
rows.abstract: Process-based hydrological models have advantages in representing physical mechanisms, whereas deep learning models excel at capturing complex nonlinear relationships. Effectively integrating these complementary strengths remains a key issue in runoff modeling. To address this issue, this study develops BiGRU-dXAJ, a differentiable hybrid hydrological model that places XAJ parameter learning within a multi-catchment joint training framework. The framework reformulates the XAJ model as differentiable tensor operations and couples it with a shared BiGRU-based parameter learning network. Meteorological forcings and static catchment attributes are jointly used to infer hydrological parameters, enabling end-to-end optimization of parameter learning and runoff simulation. Large-sample evaluation shows that dynamic-parameter BiGRU-dXAJ outperforms deep learning models, the traditional XAJ model, and static-parameter hybrid models. Spatial generalization experiments indicate promising but region-dependent performance in ungauged basins. The learned dynamic parameters generally follow the physical meanings defined in the XAJ model. Overall, differentiable hybrid modeling shows potential for runoff simulation.

rows.title: Integrating MSPA and circuit theory to identify a flood risk transmission path and construction grading control network: A case study of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region
rows.abstract: Flood disasters are increasingly severe under global climate change, traditional flood risk assessment methods often overlook the interactions between natural and social factors, limiting their capacity to capture risk generation and transfer processes. To address this gap, this study integrates Morphological Spatial Pattern Analysis (MSPA) and Circuit Theory (CT), treating flood inundation areas as risk sources, analogizing the interaction between natural and social factors as a "Resistance network" and "Current" as a "Flood flow", and constructs a graded flood risk control network consisting of "Core risk sources-Flood corridors-Key nodes". Taking the July 2023 flood disaster in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei (BTH) region as a case study, the network identified 24 primary and 73 secondary risk sources, 253 transmission corridors, 327 pinch points, and 300 barrier points. Based on these findings, a chain-type prevention and control strategy of “Source control-Process interruption-Terminal regulation” was proposed.

rows.title: Global-RSWQmonitor: Global water quality mapping and monitoring with Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery on Google Earth Engine cloud platform
rows.abstract: Monitoring inland and coastal water quality at large spatial scales and near-real-time frequency remains challenging because accessible cloud-based tools remain limited. We present Global-RSWQmonitor, an interactive Google Earth Engine (GEE) application for mapping and monitoring key water quality parameters worldwide. The platform integrates Landsat-8/9 and Sentinel-2 observations, incorporates ACOLITE-based atmospheric correction through a hybrid GEE workflow, and evaluates different atmospheric correction options for aquatic remote sensing. Chlorophyll-a, turbidity, total suspended solids, colored dissolved organic matter, and Secchi disk depth are retrieved using empirical models calibrated with the global GLORIA in-situ database. Validation against field measurements from representative lakes shows that the retrieved parameters capture major water quality patterns with reliable performance. By combining cloud computing, multi-sensor satellite archives, and a Python-based interface, Global-RSWQmonitor supports retrospective analysis, interactive visualization, and near-real-time water quality monitoring at global scales. The application is freely accessible at here.

rows.title: What structured tool interfaces do and do not provide for LLM-based SWAT+ calibration
rows.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly coupled with scientific simulators, yet how structured tool interfaces affect operational reliability and decision provenance remains unclear. This study introduces Hydro-MCP, a Model Context Protocol framework that constrains LLM-mediated SWAT + operation through typed function schemas, parameter-range validation, structured diagnostic feedback, and trajectory logging. We evaluated Hydro-MCP using a six-level ablation in the urban Jungnangcheon watershed, reference baselines, a rural Jiseokcheon stress test, and a held-out corruption task. In the permissive Jungnangcheon benchmark, the full Hydro-MCP configuration followed a shorter evaluation path within the tested workflow, 21.9 ± 5.3 versus 62.0 ± 16.5 model evaluations relative to unstructured LLM operation (p < 0.001), while terminal performance remained nearly unchanged (monthly NSE ≈ 0.893). A random-search baseline required fewer evaluations but achieved slightly lower terminal NSE, indicating that Hydro-MCP improves LLM-guided operation rather than non-LLM sampling efficiency. In Jiseokcheon, the full configuration achieved operational completion in all runs and Level 1 in 7 of 10 runs, whereas Levels 2-3 initiated no SWAT + simulation. This completion result concerns access to and execution of the workflow; the subsequent KGE, terminal parameters, and process-consistency analysis separately exposed zombie calibration despite acceptable fit. The corruption task further showed that logs and range constraints alone cannot detect physically corrupted model states. Within the tested workflow, the full Hydro-MCP configuration therefore improved operational control and produced reviewable provenance, while hydrological validity still required process-level consistency checks.

rows.title: Large language models for water distribution systems modeling and decision-making
rows.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into engineering workflows presents new opportunities for making computational tools more accessible, especially where such tools remain underutilized due to technical or expertise barriers, such as water distribution system (WDS) management. This study introduces LLM-EPANET, an agent-based framework that enables natural language interaction with EPANET, the benchmark WDS simulator. The framework combines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and multi-agent orchestration to automatically translate user queries into executable code, run simulations, and return structured results. A curated set of 69 benchmark queries is introduced to evaluate performance across state-of-the-art LLMs. Results show that LLMs can effectively support a wide range of modeling tasks, achieving 56–81% accuracy overall and over 90% for simpler queries, highlighting the potential of LLM-based modeling to support broader accessibility of data-driven tools and advance the democratization of water systems modeling through transparent, interactive AI interfaces. The framework code and benchmark queries are shared as an open resource.

rows.title: Leveraging digital twins for urban health and sustainability: A case study for urban air quality management in Manhattan
rows.abstract: Urban health and sustainability management is essential for residents, which requires data analytics and visualization tools for decision support. Digital twins are real-time virtual replicas that can map the states and behaviors of physical entities and environments in urban systems. This study proposes a digital twin framework for urban health and sustainability and builds a large-scale air quality management prototype system in Manhattan. The framework comprises: (i) a data-collection module that acquires, cleans, and time-aligns multidimensional streams from CO2/pollutant monitors and other IoT sources, with device metadata, geospatial referencing, and quality-control routines; (ii) an interactive frontend with a 3D digital-twin dashboard, multiscale emissions analytics, and dynamic heatmaps for hotspot detection; and (iii) a backend that couples a Unity WebGL model with a Bayesian spatiotemporal estimator in a state-space formulation. The prototype supports CO2-focused environmental monitoring, spatial analysis, and exploratory scenario evaluation by integrating heterogeneous data, uncertainty-aware estimation, and interactive visualization.

rows.title: LagEnsembleForecasting: Multi-lag ensemble learning and cross-pollutant transfer learning for comprehensive air quality forecasting
rows.abstract: Accurate air pollution forecasting is critical for public health and environmental management. Two challenges persist: (1) selecting appropriate lagged input sequences capturing both short-term and long-term pollutant dynamics, and (2) inefficient isolated modeling for each pollutant, limiting scalability. We introduce LagEnsembleForecasting, a deep ensemble framework addressing these challenges. Our approach combines four LSTM-based models trained on distinct lagged sequences (1 h, 6 h, 12 h, 24 h), producing point forecasts and uncertainty estimates (mean ± standard deviation) evaluated across 10 independent random seeds to ensure statistical robustness. This captures short-term fluctuations and broader accumulation trends. Initially developed for PM2.5 forecasting, where the framework achieves a mean MAE of 11.66 ± 0.15μg/m3 and R2 of 0.9548 ± 0.0004 with the tightest confidence interval across all evaluated architectures, models are fine-tuned for additional pollutants (PM10, SO2, CO, O3, NO2), leveraging transfer learning to avoid retraining. Fine-tuning achieves MAE improvements of 8.51%–11.21% over from-scratch baselines across all target pollutants (p<0.001, Bonferroni-corrected), while requiring only half the training epochs and a ten-fold lower learning rate. Experiments on Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality data show LagEnsembleForecasting outperforms single lag-specific models and from-scratch baselines. Results confirm the effectiveness of combining multi-lag ensemble modeling with cross-pollutant transfer learning for real-time forecasting, directly aligned with the increasingly stringent requirements of regulatory frameworks such as the WHO 2021 Air Quality Guidelines and EU Directive 2024/2881/EU.

rows.title: Negotiating management alternatives under uncertain future conditions using a self-organizing map framework
rows.abstract: Evaluating the performance of environmental management alternatives requires balancing stakeholder objectives under a wide array of plausible States of the World (SOWs). This paper contributes the MAPS (Mapping Alternative Performance across SOWs) framework, a visual decision-support approach that uses Self-Organizing Maps (SOMs), which simultaneously perform clustering and dimension reduction, to help stakeholders compare management alternatives under deep uncertainty. MAPS clusters large ensembles of SOWs into interpretable groups arranged on a two-dimensional map, onto which alternatives’ performance is superimposed. This enables stakeholders to examine how performance varies across conditions, where their goals are met or missed, and how objective tradeoffs are shifted across the plausible space of system conditions. The framework is demonstrated with a Colorado River Basin case study, illustrating how MAPS can identify potential conflict zones between Upper and Lower Basin stakeholders and lead to identification of compromise alternatives.

rows.title: Information loss over hillslope flowpaths and scaling from urban runoff models
rows.abstract: We propose a novel approach for computing information loss in a watershed based on flow accumulation that physically explains how hydrologically driven information changes with spatial scale. Modifying Shannon’s joint entropy to incorporate flow accumulation over progressively downstream regions of a watershed, the Watershed Joint Entropy index reveals patterns of homogeneity and heterogeneity at different scales across the watershed. A normalized joint entropy expression computed along the longest flow path reflects changes in information loss or gain with cumulative contributing area. Demonstrated on a small watershed with diverse land use, terrain and soil type the approach quantifies information change and landscape diversity along the river network. The same behaviour is confirmed in five additional watersheds with urban land cover ranging from 8% to 58%. The fuzzy Jaccard similarity index in conjunction with flowrates and volumes computed using lumped and distributed applications of standard urban runoff models demonstrate that the proposed measures are able to determine watershed specific scaling thresholds given the spatial distribution of hydrological processes in the catchment.

rows.title: Exploring graph neural networks for flood modeling: Challenges, opportunities, and future prospects
rows.abstract: Hydrodynamic flood models play a central role in understanding the spatiotemporal evolution of floods for effective disaster management. Current implementations are limited, as physics-based numerical models are constrained by slow inference times, and data-driven models lack interpretability and physical consistency. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) provide a physically meaningful framework to represent unstructured spatial domains as graphs, mirroring the node-link structure of numerical models. Unlike other deep learning methods, GNNs require no complex spatial data transformation and can seamlessly integrate physics-based priors. This review synthesizes forty nine peer-reviewed studies on GNN applications in flood modeling, identifying key gaps in physics incorporation, scalability, and cross-domain generalization. Drawing on advances from related fields where GNNs have excelled, we outline strategies to overcome these limitations. GNNs hold significant potential as next-generation flood models by combining physical realism, computational efficiency, and adaptability for real-time flood prediction and risk management.

rows.title: GeoNavigator: An agent-based intelligent download tool for Earth Surface System open science entity data
rows.abstract: Earth Surface System (ESS) open science data sharing platforms have been established globally. However, these platforms differ substantially in their access mechanisms, authentication procedures, query conventions, and front-end interactions, making cross-platform data acquisition difficult to automate through a single workflow. A structured survey of 26 representative ESS data platforms found that nine platforms (34.62%) provide neither a documented API nor a provider-supported SDK and rely exclusively on Web Portal access, while the available programmatic interfaces remain platform-specific. This paper designs and implements GeoNavigator, an agent-based intelligent download tool that provides a unified natural-language entry point for heterogeneous ESS data portals, regardless of whether programmatic access is available. GeoNavigator supports login, verification, querying, downloading, and local data validation within a single workflow. The Spatial-Aware DOM represents node semantics and viewport-level spatial features as structured observations for the LLM. Expert experience and distilled successful trajectories provide operational guidance and reduce repeated exploration. Across 84 retrieval tasks on seven ESS data platforms, GeoNavigator achieved a task success rate of 95.24% and a download accuracy of 94.05%. Tests with seven foundation models yielded success rates ranging from 70% to 90%, indicating compatibility with the evaluated model interfaces. These results demonstrate the feasibility of providing a common natural-language task interface across heterogeneous ESS portals, while the verified output files can be used in existing data-processing and modelling workflows.

rows.title: GreenHub: Toward an open platform for machine learning-based crop yield modeling and deployment
rows.abstract: Agricultural researchers face challenges in publishing and sharing data-driven crop yield models, limiting transparency and collaboration. Additionally, collecting and preprocessing data from diverse sources is often inefficient. We present GreenHub, a first step toward a platform that streamlines both data access and model deployment for crop yield forecasting. GreenHub provides (i) public access to standardized, high-quality datasets; (ii) a uniform interface and Python-based library for flexible data retrieval; and (iii) hosting of machine learning models. Data sources include weather forecasts, soil properties, and vegetation indices. Researchers can upload models with minimal integration effort, and the platform automatically executes and visualizes model predictions for public access. This enables model comparison and fosters collaboration while saving researcher’s time. By lowering technical barriers, GreenHub offers an efficient ecosystem that lays the groundwork for developing, deploying, and sharing crop yield prediction models.

rows.title: A PCA-based similarity-window framework for vegetation drought-threshold detection and driver-shift assessment in Northwest China
rows.abstract: Dryland vegetation may shift abruptly when growing-season precipitation falls below critical levels, yet whether threshold crossing reorganizes vegetation controls remains unclear. We developed a PCA-based similarity-window drought-threshold framework to detect vegetation drought thresholds in Northwest China using 2001–2024 NDVI and growing-season precipitation records. Interpretable XGBoost-SHAP models compared driver importance before and after threshold crossing, and the CMIP6 model INM-CM5-0 estimated late-century changes in threshold-crossing risk under SSP1-2.6, SSP2-4.5, and SSP5-8.5. Significant thresholds occurred in 32.36% of valid vegetated pixels, with a median precipitation threshold of 285.15 mm; 42.59% occurred below the local 20th percentile, indicating that a substantial fraction of responses emerged only under severe drying. Temperature importance increased by 51.9% after threshold crossing. Future risk changes were spatially heterogeneous and stronger under SSP5-8.5, with risk-increase hotspots in eastern Qinghai and southern Gansu. The framework supports ecological drought monitoring.

rows.title: Are we eliciting the right preferences? Insights from spatial MCDA sensitivity and uncertainty analysis
rows.abstract: Planning support systems (PSS) based on geographic information systems (GIS) and multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) are sensitive to uncertainties in input parameters, yet these are often overlooked, with attention mainly on objective weighting. This study applies uncertainty analysis and Sobol global sensitivity analysis to assess key preference-related uncertainties in the Spatial Suitability Analysis Tool (SSANTO), a GIS-MCDA PSS for blue-green infrastructure (BGI) planning. We examined weights of objective, attribute value scales and the additivity parameter (γ) of the aggregation function, which controls how individual attributes are combined into overall suitability. Using spatially explicit Sobol analysis with 90,000 Monte Carlo simulations, we showed a limited subset of parameters drives outcomes: γ is dominant, followed by weights of objective, while value scales have minor effects. Spatial sensitivity is important, as low-average contributors may exert strong local effects. These findings guide parameter prioritization, data collection, and design of robust, transparent GIS-MCDA workflows, providing a framework for analyzing preference uncertainties.

rows.title: Quantitative assessment method of connectivity resilience in natural-artificial water systems in the piedmont transition zone: A watershed application for extreme climate
rows.abstract: Connecting rivers and lakes can enhance regional water security, but artificial regulation may reshape ecological robustness. Focusing on the Feng River Basin, a mountain–plain transition zone, this study develops a directed topological network linking natural rivers and engineered canals and proposes a four-dimensional Structure–Connectivity–Function–Resilience (SCFR) framework. Driven by SWAT-based multi-scenario simulations, the framework quantifies the effects of drought stress and human intervention on composite water-network resilience. Results show that artificial systems expanded physical extent but reduced circularity, node connectivity rate, and overall connectivity by 11.83%, 3.04%, and 6.63%, respectively. Under extreme drought, ecological security rate and water system connection rate decreased by 7.68% and 1.68%, respectively, while recovery time increased by 0.622 days. Current water allocation measures did not fully offset resilience losses caused by artificial intervention. The SCFR framework developed in this study provides quantitative support for water system zoning, risk node identification, and connectivity regulation.

rows.title: CliaN: An interactive graphical interface tool for climate network construction and analysis
rows.abstract: Climate network analysis is increasingly used to study complex interactions in Earth's climate system, but constructing networks from gridded data remains difficult because existing tools often require manual preprocessing and programming expertise. We present CliaN, a Windows desktop application with an interactive graphical user interface for climate network construction and analysis from gridded climate datasets. CliaN provides a complete workflow for NetCDF data import and preprocessing, network construction with cross-correlation, event synchronization, and event coincidence analysis, and the computation, visualization, and export of network metrics. Validation against published South American rainfall and simplified Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature benchmarks shows that CliaN reliably reproduces event-based and cross-correlation networks. Runtime benchmarks further quantify desktop performance across spatial resolutions and show that CliaN runs event synchronization faster than the tested Python implementation. CliaN therefore lowers the technical barrier to reproducible and efficient climate network analysis for a broader community.

rows.title: Structural investigation of regime-dependent surrogate representations under controlled hydrodynamic conditions: A Mixture-of-Experts approach
rows.abstract: Rapid flood mapping requires surrogate models capable of approximating computationally expensive two-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations, but monolithic networks may smooth regime-dependent wetting–drying and floodplain-activation responses. This study evaluates a conditional Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) surrogate that decomposes discharge–inundation mappings into specialized expert responses through learned gating. Using 43 synthetic TELEMAC-2D flood simulations of the Lower Piura River Basin (Peru), sampled at 5-minute temporal resolution and exported to 10-m raster grids, the MoE was tested under a scenario-disjoint partition against a single-expert baseline. On unseen hydrographs, the four-expert MoE improved CSI from 0.7915 to 0.8323, reduced depth loss from 0.0127 to 0.0103 m, and reduced relative volume error from 0.1209 to 0.1024. Gate trajectories suggested hydrograph-phase specialization, while ablations indicated that peak performance required combining conditional gating, inundation-state supervision, and physics-regularized learning.

rows.title: Including rainfall sequencing and autocorrelation adjustment as a component of bias correction for hydroclimate projections
rows.abstract: Bias correction of rainfall data is often required for the production of hydroclimate projections due to the misestimation of important characteristics of the precipitation process in global and/or regional climate models. Most bias correction methods ignore rainfall sequencing and correct the daily distribution only, which can lead to biases in runoff characteristics when corrected rainfall is used as an input into hydrological models. A bias correction method (RhoQM) is developed in which rainfall sequencing is corrected using estimated autocorrelation functions from autoregressive-moving average (ARMA) models. We correct historical and future rainfall from an ensemble of regional climate models for south-eastern Australia and compare the results to standard quantile-quantile mapping. Correctly specifying the autocorrelation function complexity can reduce residual cross-validated bias in rainfall and runoff metrics. There is little difference in future change signal in metrics from different model complexities, which suggests that the method is robust for hydroclimate projections.

rows.title: An interpretable multi-horizon forecasting framework for daily urban CO2 emissions using multisource social sensing data
rows.abstract: Low-frequency inventories limit near-real-time urban CO2 management. This study develops an interpretable, reusable framework that integrates multisource social-sensing signals into SARIMAX models for daily city-scale CO2 emission forecasting. Daily Carbon Monitor emissions are combined with Baidu search intensity, Weibo-derived sentiment indicators, and topic features, and evaluated for 1- to 49-day-ahead forecasts under an operational no-look-ahead design. Tianjin is used for model development, while Shanghai and Chongqing provide external municipal validation over a common 821-day window from 1 January 2023 to 31 March 2025. The full social-sensing specification reduces mean RMSE relative to the history-only baseline by 10.36% in Tianjin, 9.77% in Shanghai, and 9.64% in Chongqing. GRU and TCN benchmarks show that social-sensing inputs do not automatically improve nonlinear sequence models. Social sensing is therefore interpreted as an event-attention and public-response layer for high-frequency urban carbon decision support.

rows.title: Explainable residual learning for diagnosing infiltration model limitations: A Loess Plateau case study
rows.abstract: The structural adequacy of classic infiltration models remains uncertain in non-stationary small watersheds. This study developed a diagnostic hybrid framework combining mechanism-enhanced infiltration models, Random Forest (RF)/Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) residual learning, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) interpretation. The framework was applied to 35 runoff events in the Xindiangou watershed on China's Loess Plateau using modified Horton, Philip, and Green-Ampt models. RF/XGBoost residual learning improved calibration-period performance, but validation gains were model-dependent, indicating limited transferability. SHAP analysis identified model-specific residual signatures: Horton residuals were mainly linked to total rainfall, Philip residuals to maximum hourly rainfall intensity and vegetation conditions, and Green-Ampt residuals to antecedent wetness. Parameter–SHAP correlations suggested retrospective parameter compensation, especially for Green-Ampt. Bootstrap and collinearity diagnostics supported stable leading SHAP signals but required cautious group-level interpretation. Overall, explainable residual learning provides case-specific evidence to guide targeted refinement of infiltration models.

rows.title: Multiple machine-learning estimation of groundwater levels and trends for the regional Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer
rows.abstract: The Mississippi River Valley alluvial aquifer provides irrigation, public, and domestic water supplies across the south-central United States. Declining groundwater levels require improved characterization of changing conditions. Traditional potentiometric-surface mapping does not use all available water-level data or quantify uncertainty. To address these limitations, we developed a data-driven multiple machine-learning (MML) framework delivered through two open-source R packages. The covMRVAgen1 software assembles covariates to 155,960 monthly groundwater levels from 57,695 wells; the mmlMRVAgen1 software trains Cubist and Random Forest models, blends them, and makes 1-kilometer gridded predictions of monthly potentiometric surfaces for the period January 1980–December 2022. The MML approach provides a methodological foundation for region-scale spatiotemporal groundwater prediction and uncertainty quantification, generating 90-percent prediction limits with appropriate empirical coverage. Model performance is acceptable, with a root-mean-square error of about 4.2 feet, standard deviation of 24.82 feet, and a normalized Nash–Sutcliffe efficiency of 0.973.

rows.title: Editorial Board
Watershed-agnostic modeling: An explainable, distributed, data-driven hydrologic model
rows.abstract: Reliable streamflow modeling is critical as climate change increases variability. This study introduces a data-driven framework that combines Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers to estimate next-day discharge across a dense network of Michigan gauges. The method directly ingests multi-day gridded weather layers, eliminating the need for watershed delineation or other hydrologic preprocessing, and functioning as a digital analog to a distributed process model. When trained on a decade-long record, the network achieved predominantly “good” to “very good” Nash–Sutcliffe and Kling–Gupta efficiencies at most stations, out-performing alternative spatial or temporal clustering approaches in reproducing established atmospheric and ecoregional patterns. Gradient-based saliency, supported by a targeted spatial-perturbation experiment, shows that the model focuses on hydrologically plausible source regions, providing physical interpretability to its estimates. These findings show that pixel-level CNN-LSTM architectures provide skillful, transparent, and efficient streamflow guidance suitable for basin-scale water resource decision support.

rows.title: Ilya M. Sobol’ (1926–2025): The question that shaped global sensitivity analysis
rows.abstract: The passing of Ilya M. Sobol’ marks the loss of an influential mathematician whose work pioneered and fundamentally shaped global sensitivity analysis (GSA) and modern uncertainty quantification. This tribute reflects on Sobol's foundational role in GSA, with particular emphasis on the variance-based framework, now widely known as the Sobol’ method. Drawing on historical context and personal recollections from two of his long-time colleagues, it honors Sobol's scientific and human legacy while considering the continuing importance of sensitivity analysis for understanding increasingly complex and integrated models under uncertainty.

rows.title: Driving analysis of the continuous groundwater decline along the lower Yellow River: Lagged contributions of natural and human factors (2001–2020)
rows.abstract: The high-sediment perched lower Yellow River forms a distinctive river-aquifer system, with groundwater decline along its banks over the past two decades. Using 2001–2020 data, a framework integrating Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess (STL) and an attention-enhanced Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and lag-response was constructed. STL indicated that long-term trends explained 53.12%–91.35% of groundwater-level variance, reflecting a trend-dominated decline. Model applicability varied with spatial and hydrogeological constraints: STL-LSTM resolved periodic near-river seepage (0–5 km; R2 = 0.888), whereas attention-enhanced LSTM improved predictions in pumped far-river zones (>10 km; R2 = 0.816). Driver attribution revealed spatial distance-decay in groundwater responses.
